papers.title: Spatial multiomics identifies rheumatoid arthritis synovial niches and de-novo laminar histological patterns of fibroblasts subtypes.
papers.abstract: IntroductionSpatial omic technologies provide insight into molecular architecture and spatial cellular organization within tissue. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), single-cell RNA sequencing and low-resolution spatial transcriptomics have advanced the understanding of synovial biology. However, single-cell spatial resolution using multiple spatial platforms to comprehensively map the immune and stromal cell organization as well as topographical cellular interactions in the RA synovium remain limited.MethodsWe integrated single-cell and bulk spatial transcriptomics (CosMx and Xenium, and Visium, respectively) as well as spatial LC/MS proteomics and a multiplex immunohistochemical protein panel in the histological evaluation of a non-clinical cohort of six RA, three osteoarthritis (OA) and three healthy (NH) arthroscopic synovial biopsies. The histopathological observations were integrated with Xenium-based spatial computational analyses in the RA and NH synovium to define fibroblast organization and spatial relationships in RA compared to the NH synovium.ResultsCross-platform comparisons demonstrated a strong concordance in cellular composition and microanatomical localization and highlighted the strengths of each technology, with single-cell spatial analysis providing higher cellular resolution, but reduced molecular depth. Comparison of single-cell spatial transcriptomics and LC/MS proteomics also demonstrated concordance, but revealed region-specific expression of fibroblast-associated genes and proteins. Spatial mapping in our large biopsies identified a previously unrecognized laminar organization of up to nine fibroblast subtypes spanning the lining and sublining regions of RA synovium, distinct from NH. Spatial computational pathology analyses showed that specific fibroblast subtypes preferentially localized within lymphoid (CD74+ and CXCL12+), vascular (NOTCH3+ and mural) and stromal (POSTN+, DKK3+ and CD34+) niches. Pathway enrichment analyses further implicated specific biological functions to the fibroblast subtypes that were linked to their microenvironment.ConclusionThis multimodal spatial molecular pathology study indicates that in RA, fibroblast subtypes expand, spatially reorganize, and establish specialized tissue niches that likely contribute to disease pathogenesis. These findings provide a high-resolution spatial framework and support future spatial multiomics studies aimed at identifying fibroblast ecotypes in the context of treatment naïve, treatment-responsive and treatment-refractory RA patients to identify tissue-level spatial signatures associated with inadequate response to treatments.

papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of cellular heterogeneity in Alzheimer disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is defined neuropathologically by the presence of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, yet these canonical lesions alone cannot account for its clinical, regional and cellular heterogeneity. AD is a multicellular, spatially organized disease shaped by the interactions of neurons, glia and vascular cells within distinct anatomical microenvironments. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing have made it possible to dissect the transcriptional signatures of individual cell populations in the AD brain, revealing selective neuronal vulnerability, stage-dependent glial remodelling and widespread disruption of cell-cell communication networks, whereas spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed imaging have anchored these molecular changes to their tissue context. Studies of defined populations, such as people with autosomal-dominant AD or Down syndrome-associated AD, and of the oldest-old cohorts help disentangle the molecular changes that are causal drivers from those that are downstream consequences. Across individuals, AD heterogeneity is further shaped by sex and ancestry, underscoring the need for broader representation of these factors in single-cell and spatial studies. These advances are also reshaping translational pipelines through multi-omic benchmarking of animal models and single-cell-based drug-repurposing strategies. Thus, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are redefining our understanding of AD heterogeneity and informing precision approaches to treatment.

papers.title: TWEAK signaling drives the transition from psoriasis to atopic dermatitis-like inflammation in paradoxical eczema.
papers.abstract: Targeted biologics have transformed the treatment of inflammatory skin diseases such as plaque psoriasis. However, some patients with psoriasis paradoxically develop eczematous skin reactions after therapy targeting tumor necrosis factor (TNF), interleukin-17 (IL-17), or IL-23. Although paradoxical eczema (PE) resembles atopic dermatitis (AD) clinically and histologically, the molecular mechanisms that drive its development remain poorly understood. Here, we generated high-resolution cellular and spatial maps of human skin using single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, immunohistochemistry, and in vitro assays, profiling lesional biopsies from patients with PE (n = 8 donors), alongside healthy control, psoriasis, and AD skin (n = 4 donors per group). In PE, we identified distinct transcriptional changes characterized by myeloid and T cell expansion and an altered keratinocyte phenotype shaped by TNF-like weak inducer of apoptosis (TWEAK; encoded by TNFSF12) signaling through its receptor TNFRSF12A, confirmed at the protein level by immunohistochemistry. To define the underlying mechanism, we stimulated immortalized (N-TERT) and primary human keratinocytes and found that TWEAK acted together with IL-13 to drive a T helper 2- and type I interferon-polarized epithelial program that partially recapitulated the keratinocyte signature of PE lesions. We validated key target genes by quantitative polymerase chain reaction in primary keratinocytes. In THP-1 cells and primary human CD14+ monocytes, anti-TNF treatment induced TWEAK expression, suggesting a compensatory inflammatory circuit. Together, these findings identify the TWEAK-IL-13 axis as a key driver of PE and suggest how cytokine blockade may reshape cutaneous immune responses.

papers.title: Spatially integrated transcriptomics maps the metastatic niche in lymph nodes of gastric cancer.
papers.abstract: Lymph node (LN) metastasis is a major determinant of clinical outcome in gastric cancer (GC), yet the molecular and spatial features of metastatic LN niches remain incompletely defined. Here, we integrated digital spatial profiling (DSP) of primary GC and matched LNs, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and 10x Genomics Visium spatial transcriptomics. Cross-sectional analysis of cytokeratin-positive regions across primary GC and N1-N3 metastatic lymph nodes (mLNs) identified a hybrid epithelial-mesenchymal expression pattern in N1 samples and prominent immune checkpoint, angiogenic, and receptor tyrosine kinase programs in the N3 group. Deconvolution showed enrichment of exhausted T cells, regulatory T cells, and fibroblasts in mLNs, consistent with immunosuppressive remodeling of the local microenvironment. Cell-cell communication analysis implicated the galectin-9 (LGALS9)-CD45/CD44, CLEC2D-KLRB1, and CCL19/CCL21-CCR7 axes in mLNs. Spatial analysis further revealed compartment-specific heterogeneity, including distinct proliferative, immune, and immunosuppressive programs. Integrating multiple transcriptomic datasets, we derived a 12-gene lymph node metastasis gene signature (LNMGS); high LNMGS scores were associated with poorer overall survival in the TCGA-STAD cohort. Spatial mapping of the LNMGS in primary GC identified an LNMGS-high region displaying a center-to-periphery expression gradient and tending to have a higher inferred copy-number burden. A distance-associated gene signature derived from this gradient was enriched for proliferation, invasion, angiogenesis, immune evasion, and stemness. Together, these findings provide a spatial and molecular framework for lymph node metastasis in GC and highlight potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for further investigation. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

papers.title: Human hair-bearing skin organoids reveal cell type-specific susceptibility and innate immune responses to herpes simplex virus 1.
papers.abstract: Epithelial surfaces are the primary sites of lytic herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection following initial exposure or reactivation from latency. To model this complex environment, we used human hair-bearing skin organoids and combined single-cell spatial transcriptomics with imaging to map viral spread and host responses across skin architecture. Our data suggest delayed progression of the HSV-1 life cycle in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicle cells compared to the dermis. Infection triggered spatially organized host responses, including induction of IER3 in papillary fibroblasts. In basal keratinocytes, IRF3 was up-regulated in both infected and neighboring uninfected cells, consistent with paracrine activation of antiviral signaling. Inflammatory responses were compartmentalized in a cell type-specific manner, with TNFSF9 (4-1BBL) induced in papillary fibroblasts and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) induced in keratinocytes. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays confirmed secretion of these cytokines and the TNF-α-responsive chemokines CXCL2 and CXCL10. CXCL2 expression was enriched in cells adjacent to TNF-α-expressing cells, highlighting spatial coordination of inflammatory signaling. While interferon-β reduced viral replication, TNF-α and 4-1BBL did not, suggesting that their primary role is to orchestrate immune cell recruitment and activation. These findings establish human hair-bearing skin organoids as a physiologically relevant model for investigating spatial host-HSV-1 interactions.

papers.title: Spatial and single-cell insights into the prostate cancer microenvironment: overcoming immunotherapy resistance through multidimensional strategies.
papers.abstract: Despite breakthroughs in immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) across various malignancies, prostate cancer (PCa), particularly metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), has shown limited responses to ICIs. This pervasive primary resistance is fundamentally driven by the canonically "immune-cold" and highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) of PCa. Propelled by recent advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, this review comprehensively deconstructs the dynamic spatiotemporal evolution of the PCa immune landscape across localized, mCRPC, and lineage-plastic variant stages (e.g., neuroendocrine and double-negative PCa). We systematically delineate how the profound immune-excluded phenotype is sculpted not by isolated events, but by an intricate, multicellular suppressive ecosystem. Specifically, we detail the subclonal heterogeneity, spatial topography, and metabolic crosstalk of key suppressive populations, including specific tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) subsets, regulatory T cells (Tregs), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Furthermore, we elucidate the tumor-intrinsic genetic aberrations (e.g., PTEN inactivation, TP53 mutations) and epigenetic rewiring (e.g., EZH2, CHD1, ARID1A dysregulation) that initiate and perpetually orchestrate this suppressive network. Finally, we highlight emerging therapeutic vulnerabilities and future translational directions. Dismantling the microenvironmental barriers in PCa necessitates transcending singular ICI blockade by employing novel combinatorial strategies that target chemotactic recruitment axes (e.g., CXCR2/CXCR4), reverse metabolic plasticity, and abrogate epigenetic silencing. Coupled with high-resolution liquid biopsy biomarkers (e.g., ctDNA, B7-H3+ EVs) for precise patient stratification and cutting-edge synthetic biology interventions, these multidimensional approaches hold profound promise for reversing the dual metabolic and immune suppressive state of PCa, thereby overcoming clinical immunotherapy resistance.

papers.title: Lattice and Triply Periodic Minimal Surface Architectures for Dental Implants: A Scoping Review of Design, Manufacturing, and Performance.
papers.abstract: Dental implant longevity depends on both biological integration and mechanical compatibility with bone. Dense titanium and Ti-6Al-4V implants are far stiffer than peri-implant bone, a mismatch that promotes stress shielding and marginal bone loss. Architected lattice and triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) structures, enabled by additive manufacturing (AM), lower effective stiffness and create interconnected space for bone ingrowth, vascularization, and osseointegration, yet the value of any single architecture is hard to isolate because geometry, density, material, processing, and surface state act together. This scoping review maps the evidence on lattice and TPMS dental implants and how design strategy, AM route, and material system govern mechanical reliability and biological validation. Studies were charted by material, architecture, AM route, model scale (15 full implants, three implant-like or root-analogue models, 10 scaffold or coupon specimens), validation level (L1-L5) and outcome. Across the 28 included studies, titanium and Ti-6Al-4V dominate (19 studies, 12 of them fabricated by laser powder bed fusion), while zirconia from vat-based ceramic routes emerges as an esthetic, biologically promising alternative (six studies). The evidence remains uneven: 24 studies included simulation, 16 physical mechanical testing, 11 in vitro biology, three in vivo validation and only two a fatigue endpoint, and none reached clinical-level evidence. A lattice implant thus behaves as the combined product of its material, architecture, process, and surface; progress depends on reporting manufactured geometry, demonstrating fatigue and debris safety, and pairing in vitro with in vivo osseointegration. On the present evidence base, architecture-level statements are best read as design hypotheses and evidence trends rather than as clinically preferred configurations.

papers.title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington's disease.
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT), yet how somatic repeat instability and HTT inclusions relate to selective cell loss in the human brain remains unclear. We have developed a multimodal spatial transcriptomics approach that enables the definition of transcriptional programs with subcellular resolution, somatic CAG repeat lengths, and eight other pathology markers, including HTT inclusions, in every cell of intact brain sections. Imaging 428,173 cells in the control and HD cortex revealed the selective vulnerability of layer 5-6 (L5-6) near-projecting (NP) neurons and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons, which undergo a >50% loss that is closely linked to large somatic repeat expansions (>450 ± 55 CAGs). Intranuclear inclusions were most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansions (250-350 CAGs) and were associated with broader transcriptional changes than somatic repeat expansion alone. These data provide a comprehensive resource and establish a general framework for connecting repeat expansion and protein pathology across diverse cell types.

papers.title: Targeting the Immunometabolic Checkpoint IL4I1 Suppresses the Progression of Pathological Scars.
papers.abstract: Keloids are refractory fibroproliferative disorders driven by dysregulated fibrosis and chronic inflammation. Current research has largely focused on the TGF-β signaling pathway and fibroblasts-the classical drivers of keloid formation-yet clinical outcomes remain unsatisfactory. To address this, we shifted our research focus to the immunometabolic axis, with particular emphasis on the regulatory role of IL4I1 (an amino acid oxidase) as an immunometabolic checkpoint. Our results demonstrated that IL4I1 was significantly upregulated in keloid tissues, accompanied by activation of its mediated tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic pathway and increased downstream lipid peroxidation products. In vivo knockout of Il4i1 suppressed collagen deposition in a skin fibrosis model, confirming that IL4I1 plays a critical facilitatory role in fibrotic progression. We performed drug screening and identified L-carnosine as an inhibitor of IL4I1. L-carnosine inhibits the enzymatic activity and protein stability of IL4I1, and exhibits prominent therapeutic efficacy in a keloid nude-mouse xenograft model. Through its enzymatic activity, IL4I1 mediates dendritic-cell-driven immunometabolic reprogramming and the formation of an immunosuppressive microenvironment, consequently accelerating fibrotic progression. This study highlights IL4I1 as a therapeutic target, and its small-molecule inhibitor L-carnosine holds promise to be translated into a safe and clinically attractive therapeutic modality.

papers.title: Mapping cell-type-specific spatial gene programs uncovers tissue architecture and microenvironment organization.
papers.abstract: The complex organization of tissues is shaped by the spatial arrangement of diverse cell types executing specialized gene programs. Cell-type-specific spatial gene programs (SGPs) are transcriptional modules that capture spatial expression co-variation within cell types. However, identifying these SGPs remains challenging in spatial transcriptomics. Here we present MacSGP, a scalable framework that integrates deep graph neural networks with probabilistic modeling to identify cell-type-specific SGPs through low-rank structures while accounting for cell type mixtures. Through comprehensive simulations and real data analyses spanning diverse tissues and technologies, we demonstrate that MacSGP effectively distinguishes cell-type-specific SGPs from cell-type marker gene expression patterns while uncovering tissue architecture and cellular microenvironments. In a mouse brain dataset, we identify replicable SGPs reflecting subregional neuronal specializations, with these genes significantly enriched for heritabilities associated with brain-related phenotypes. Across colorectal cancer datasets from various platforms, MacSGP identifies consistent SGPs that define distinct cellular niches within the tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Cellular Proliferation and Reprogramming in Pre-Metastatic Niches: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Cancer metastasis, the leading cause of cancer-related mortality, fundamentally depends on the proactive remodelling of distant organ microenvironments by primary tumours through systemic signals, creating a pre-metastatic niche before tumour cell arrival. This review systematically deconstructs the dynamic spatiotemporal evolution of the pre-metastatic niche, highlighting the multi-layered reprogramming of stromal, endothelial and immune cells that collectively cultivate a pro-tumourigenic and immunosuppressive microenvironment. We elucidate the biomechanical and biochemical sensing mechanisms, derived primarily from experimental models, that dictate the fate of disseminated tumour cells, governing the critical balance between dormancy maintenance and proliferative reactivation. Furthermore, we synthesize mechanistic insights alongside human tissue and liquid-biopsy correlative evidence on how metabolic resetting and epigenetic memory may contribute to sustaining pre-metastatic niche stability, and discuss how cutting-edge single-cell and spatial omics technologies are deciphering the intricate multicellular topological architecture of the niche. Ultimately, by mapping these complex systemic interactions across preclinical, biomarker and translational levels, we identify potential therapeutic vulnerabilities and advocate for a paradigm shift toward microenvironment normalization. While clinical validation remains an evolving frontier, targeting pre-metastatic niche priming represents a promising window that warrants rigorous clinical evaluation to intercept nascent metastasis before clinically detectable colonization occurs.

papers.title: Hoxa10 governs lifelong skeletal stem cell maintenance and bone repair.
papers.abstract: Skeletal stem and progenitor cells (SSPCs) sustain bone homeostasis and regeneration throughout life, yet the transcriptional programs that preserve their identity remain poorly defined. Here we identify the distal Hox gene Hoxa10 as a cell-autonomous regulator of skeletal stem cell maintenance. Using inducible genetic deletion, lineage tracing, single-cell transcriptomics, and injury models, we show that loss of Hoxa10 leads to progressive depletion of SSPCs, impaired bone regeneration, and defective matrix organization. Mechanistically, Hoxa10 maintains the undifferentiated state of skeletal stem cells by restraining premature osteogenic, adipogenic, and chondrogenic commitment, while promoting collagen III production and collagen fiber alignment within regenerative niches. Hoxa10-dependent regulation of extracellular matrix composition is restricted to primitive progenitors and is uncoupled from osteoblast differentiation. Notably, transient depletion of distal Hox genes in primary human SSPCs recapitulates the murine defects in proliferation, self-renewal, and differentiation restraint. Together, these findings define a conserved Hox-dependent program that preserves skeletal stem cell identity and regenerative competence, revealing how developmental transcription factors are repurposed to sustain the adult skeleton across the life span.

papers.title: Cross-species single-cell and spatial transcriptomics map the conserved stromal remodeling landscape of inflammatory arthritis.

This model moves beyond traditional cellular profiling to identify therapeutic targets potentially useful towards simultaneously halting synovial inflammation and joint destruction.

papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptome analyses unveil that MYH11 links stemness to immunotherapy resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.
papers.abstract: BackgroundImmunotherapy is an essential treatment strategy for lung cancer, yet resistance to it is often unavoidable, resulting in treatment failure and poor prognosis. The cancer stem cell (CSC) theory offers a valuable perspective for understanding tumor metastasis and resistance to immunotherapy. However, there is a scarcity of multi-omics studies that identify tumor stemness subpopulations and their associated signaling pathways. In this study, we combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with spatial transcriptomics sequencing (ST-seq) to identify a myosin heavy chain 11 (MYH11)-high stemness subpopulation linked to immunotherapy resistance.MethodsWe conducted quality control and removed batch effects from two scRNA-seq datasets, then annotated cell types using established marker genes. Malignant cells were distinguished from epithelial cells with fastCNV. Stemness subpopulations were identified using a machine learning-derived messenger RNA (mRNA) stemness index (mRNAsi) and CytoTRACE analysis. To functionally characterize the stemness subpopulation, we employed Monocle3 pseudotime trajectory analysis, CellChat cell-cell communication analysis, and predicted transcription factors (TFs). We also performed consensus clustering on bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data, followed by immune-related scoring, immune cell deconvolution, and drug sensitivity prediction. Clinical validation was achieved through multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and immunohistochemistry (IHC). Experimental validation included short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated MYH11 knockdown, real-time quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) and western blot analyses, and tumor sphere formation assays to assess cancer stemness.ResultsWe identified nine major cell types and found a significant enrichment of epithelial cells in tumors resistant to immunotherapy. Using fastCNV, we identified malignant cells and defined seven malignant cell subtypes based on stemness scoring. Notably, the Stem-subtype was significantly enriched in resistant tumors. Functional analysis showed that the Stem-subtype could differentiate into other malignant cell subtypes, with a strong enrichment in the NOTCH signaling pathway. Analysis of fibroblast subpopulations revealed that MYH11 + fibroblasts were closely linked to the Stem-subtype, collectively contributing to immunotherapy resistance. Consensus clustering identified two stemness-related subtypes, with Stemness I associated with poor prognosis. Immune scoring and immune cell analysis further indicated an unfavorable response to immunotherapy in Stemness I. Drug sensitivity prediction identified potential therapeutic agents, and in silico knockout experiments revealed downstream target genes. Validation with clinical samples confirmed that MYH11-high cancer cells were closely correlated with exhausted CD8+ T cell infiltration and poor immunotherapy outcomes. Experimental validation demonstrated that MYH11 knockdown significantly reduced the expression levels of CXCL12 and TUBA1A, as well as the expression of core NOTCH pathway genes. Furthermore, the tumor sphere-forming capacity was markedly suppressed.ConclusionsIn summary, our multi-omics analysis revealed a MYH11-high malignant cell stemness subpopulation and a MYH11 + fibroblast subpopulation, both of which are closely linked to immunotherapy resistance and poor prognosis in lung cancer.

papers.title: Decoder-FFPE-seq enables sensitive, genome-wide spatial transcriptomics of archival tissues at single-cell resolution.
papers.abstract: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue-compatible spatial transcriptomics (ST) is transforming biology and histopathology, but achieving high sensitivity, genome-wide coverage, single-cell resolution, and researcher accessibility remains challenging. papers.title: An interpretable deep learning framework for revealing fine-grained spatial domains.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables gene expression profiling with preserved spatial context, yet accurate spatial domain delineation remains challenging. We present RIF, a robust and interpretable deep learning framework for fine-grained spatial domain identification. RIF leverages graph neural networks semi-supervised with pseudo-labels to preserve tissue structural integrity. It incorporates a dual-preprocessing ensemble strategy to improve model robustness and generalization. It further enables spatially variable gene detection through network interpretability. Across multiple sequencing platforms, RIF outperformed state-of-the-art comparison algorithms in spatial domain identification. In mouse brain tissue, RIF identified corresponding hippocampal subfields in the spatially separated dorsal and ventral regions and resolved the laminar organization of the olfactory bulb. In breast cancer, RIF-defined domains suggest suppressed T cell activity associated with hypoxic and oxidative microenvironments. In an invasive ductal carcinoma dataset of more than 720,000 cells, RIF-defined domains suggest an epithelial-mesenchymal transition gradient, including reduced hormone dependence and extracellular matrix remodeling.

papers.title: MIF-CD74 orchestrates synovial macrophage metabolic-inflammatory reprogramming by ENO2 interaction to drive osteoarthritis pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: Synovitis is a central driver of osteoarthritis (OA) progression, yet the cellular and molecular mechanisms sustaining inflammatory circuits in the synovium remain incompletely understood. Through integrative analysis of time-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing in murine synovium and spatial transcriptomics of human OA tissues, we identified a pathogenic CD74+ macrophage subset that expands in OA and localizes at the synovial-cartilage interface. This subset exhibits a proinflammatory, nonclassical polarization and displays a metabolic dependency on glycolysis. Multiomics and mechanistic studies revealed that CD74 interacts with the glycolytic enzyme enolase 2 (ENO2). This interaction orchestrates a feed-forward signaling axis wherein CD74/ENO2 facilitates the nuclear translocation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α (HIF-1α)/β-catenin dimers, which coactivate glycolytic and inflammatory gene programs, thereby sustaining a metabolically driven inflammatory state. Genetic ablation of CD74 in myeloid cells or its pharmacological blockade mitigated synovitis and cartilage degradation in murine OA models. To translate this axis therapeutically, we developed synovium-targeted cationic lipid nanoparticles decorated with MIF-mimetic peptides (PcLNPs) for the delivery of CD74 siRNA. Intra-articular administration of PcLNPs efficiently targeted CD74+ macrophages, attenuated their inflammatory and glycolytic phenotypes, and ameliorated murine OA progression in vivo. Our findings establish the CD74/ENO2/HIF-1α/β-catenin axis as a critical integrator of metabolic reprogramming and inflammation in OA synovitis and present a potential targeted nanotherapeutic strategy for disease modification.

papers.title: Single-cell insights into plant responses to biotic and abiotic stresses: cellular heterogeneity and regulatory mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Plants are continuously challenged by biotic and abiotic stresses that compromise growth, productivity, and stress resilience. Although bulk omics approaches have identified numerous stress-responsive pathways, they obscure the cellular heterogeneity and spatial organization that underlie stress perception, signal transmission, and response execution. Single-cell and spatial omics now enable plant stress responses to be resolved at the levels of cell type, cell state, and spatial location. In this review, we synthesize recent applications of single-cell RNA sequencing, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and emerging single-cell proteomics in plant stress biology. We systematically compare biotic and abiotic stresses in terms of spatial response patterns, cellular division of labor, cell-state transitions, and gene regulatory networks. Biotic stress typically generates localized, infection-centered immune landscapes characterized by sentinel-cell activation, vascular defense hubs, and receptor-triggered transcriptional cascades. In contrast, abiotic stress more commonly involves organ-scale homeostatic adjustment, developmental plasticity, and sustained growth-tolerance trade-offs. Despite these distinctions, both stress classes share core regulatory modules, including reactive oxygen species, hormone signaling, transcription factor networks, and vascular long-distance communication. We further discuss technical challenges related to protoplast and nuclei preparation, cell-type annotation, spatial resolution, and multimodal data integration. By linking stress-responsive genes to the specific cell types, states, and spatial domains in which they function, single-cell approaches provide a mechanistic framework for precision engineering and breeding of stress-resilient crops.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics unveils the in situ cellular and molecular hallmarks of the lung in fatal COVID-19.
papers.abstract: Severe Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can induce progressive diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) leading to fatal outcomes. Spatial organization analysis also identified specific compartmentalization including immune-specific clusters across DAD patterns. papers.title: POSTN-expressing cancer-associated fibroblasts: roles in the tumor microenvironment and clinical implications.
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are among the most abundant stromal components in the tumor microenvironment and play important roles in tumor progression, metastasis, and treatment response. Periostin (POSTN) is an extracellular matrix protein predominantly secreted by CAFs. Through crosstalk with tumor cells and diverse stromal components, POSTN+ CAFs mediate the establishment of a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment and can modulate tumor therapeutic responses. Moreover, increased POSTN expression in tumor tissues has been associated with poor prognosis in various malignancies, suggesting the potential utility of POSTN as a biomarker. However, several critical scientific questions remain to be elucidated, including the origin and plasticity of POSTN+ CAFs, their relationship with other CAF subsets, and the feasibility of targeting POSTN+ CAFs therapeutically. Notably, POSTN+ CAFs may represent a reversible fibroblast state rather than an innately determined cell lineage. In this review, we discuss the biological features and functional significance of POSTN+ CAFs in cancer, emphasizing their roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment and their potential implications for clinical practice. We further discuss current challenges and future opportunities for targeting this distinct functionally defined fibroblast state, while noting that its identity as a discrete cell population remains to be established.

papers.title: spaDWGCN: a spatial distance weighted graph convolution network for accurate spatial tissue structure identification.
papers.abstract: The continuous development of spatial transcriptomics enables us to obtain gene expression matrices alongside spatial coordinate labels for cells or spots, providing tools for understanding spatial tissue microenvironments and spatially resolved cell-cell interactions. papers.title: Bioinformatics Across the Cutaneous Scar Spectrum: Molecular States, Digital Phenotypes and Clinical Translation.
papers.abstract: Cutaneous scarring spans regenerative and normal remodelling; keloid, hypertrophic, atrophic and contractile outcomes; dyspigmentation; radiation- and inherited-fragility-associated fibrosis; and rare malignant transformation. Evidence remains concentrated in keloid and hypertrophic scar, and often reuses public datasets or extrapolates from associated cutaneous-fibrosis systems. Atrophic scars are represented mainly by quantitative imaging and treatment studies: topography and dermal loss are measurable, but no mature molecular or spatial atlas is available and atrophic acne scars are usually excluded from molecular cohorts. Scar pigmentation lacks interoperable labels, calibrated colour measurement, melanocyte-resolved spatial resources and skin-tone-stratified assessment. Fourteen studies applied artificial intelligence directly to scar data, but only one explicitly reported independent external validation. Molecular biomarkers and treatment-response models remain at discovery or internal-validation stages. papers.title: Clonal heterogeneity in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and its impact on tumor progression.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer characterized by profound desmoplasia and cellular heterogeneity, which cannot be fully resolved using traditional bulk sequencing approaches. Spatial analyses further revealed dispersed clones enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition activity and immune suppression, correlating with metastatic potential and colonization of lymph node niches. These dispersed clones shifted toward a basal phenotype, contributing to disease progression. Our findings highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, transcriptional plasticity and tumor microenvironment interactions in shaping human PDAC biology. This work provides a detailed view of the molecular and spatial heterogeneity of PDAC and offers potential avenues for therapeutic intervention targeting clonal evolution and the mechanisms driving metastasis.

papers.title: SpaCut: Transcript-Aware Morphology Fusion for Robust Cell Segmentation in Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics.
papers.abstract: Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics (SST) offers unprecedented opportunities to decipher tissue architecture at subcellular resolution. papers.title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. We present OncoSpot, a cancer-aware simulator of Visium-like spot-based ST data. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution. Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny–space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKAT, CancerFinder, Clonalscope, and RCTD revealed cancer-dependent performance: Clonalscope recovered copy-number signals more accurately in ovarian and colorectal cancer, whereas CopyKAT performed better in hepatocellular carcinoma, reflecting both the assumptions of each method and the copy-number landscapes of the three cancers. OncoSpot’s ground truth also exposed a failure mode in Clonalscope’s malignant spot identification, in which tumor and normal labels were inverted, and allowed us to trace its cause. These method-dependent behaviors would be difficult to detect in real data. OncoSpot provides a framework for benchmarking CNA inference, subclone detection, malignant spot identification, and normal spot deconvolution, and its modular design and guidelines allow extension to additional cancer types. papers.title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
papers.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression as individually localized molecules on imaging-based platforms or as counts in subcellular bins on sequencing-based platforms, and both must be assigned to cells before cell-level analysis. Existing segmentation methods focus on delineating cell boundaries, yet transcripts that diffuse beyond their cell of origin, fall where cells overlap, or lie in bins that cells only partially cover are still misassigned. Here we present Tracel, a two-stage optimal transport framework that assigns spatial observations to cells under the guidance of a matched single-cell RNA-sequencing reference. Tracel first aligns reference cells to spatial cells to estimate the expected expression profile at each cell location, and then maps transcripts to cells against these profiles. The same formulation assigns transcripts from imaging-based platforms (e.g., Xenium, CosMx) and bin counts from sequencing-based platforms (e.g., Visium HD). Across five human datasets spanning three platforms and three tissues, Tracel improves the separation of cell types over existing methods, assigning cell-type markers to their correct cells, retaining more cell-intrinsic transcripts and reducing contamination from neighboring cells. Tracel also preserves variation within cell types, yielding more accurate differential expression across spatial locations, and its expression profiles attribute ligand-receptor interactions to the correct cell-type pairs in cell-cell communication analysis. Tracel can enter the segmentation workflow at different stages, either refining an existing segmentation or segmenting cells starting from nucleus segmentation. Availability Code and example data are available at: https://tracel.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

papers.title: Peri-implant Soft Tissue Cell Behavior on Experimental β-Ti Alloys.

papers.title: The Role of Tumor-Associated Macrophages in Lung Cancer Progression and Therapy: From Mechanistic Insights to Targeting Strategies.
papers.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are among the most abundant immune cells in the lung cancer tumor microenvironment (TME), where their functions vary according to developmental origin, local signals, metabolic conditions, spatial location, and treatment exposure. The conventional M1 and M2 framework therefore does not adequately represent the diversity of macrophage states in human tumors. This narrative review examines the origin of TAMs in lung cancer, their context-dependent functional states, spatial organization, and interactions with current treatments in non-small cell lung cancer and small cell lung cancer. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have identified macrophage populations associated with primary tumors and specific metastatic sites. Mechanistic studies further implicate cytokine signalling, extracellular vesicle communication, metabolic regulation, and phagocytosis checkpoints in tumor cell proliferation, stemness maintenance, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), angiogenesis and the formation of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. TAMs can contribute to tumor clearance in some settings but promote immune suppression, tissue repair, and treatment resistance in others. Targeting strategies directed against TAMs, including inhibition of monocyte recruitment, modification of tumor-supportive macrophage states, blockade of phagocytosis checkpoints, and macrophage-directed drug delivery, have demonstrated activity primarily in experimental lung cancer models. However, clinical studies have not yet established the efficacy, selectivity, or safety of these approaches. Major challenges remain, including the high heterogeneity of TAMs, activation of compensatory pathways, systemic toxicity, and the translational gap between preclinical and clinical studies. Future research should focus on validating markers that distinguish disease-associated macrophage states from macrophages required for pulmonary homeostasis and integrating longitudinal tissue, circulating, spatial, and imaging biomarkers. Controlled clinical studies are required to determine whether macrophage-directed interventions can improve existing lung cancer treatments.

papers.title: Directionally aligned nanofibrous polycaprolactone/gelatin scaffolds as durable scleral implants for long-term ocular reconstruction.

papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic insights into neural substrates of behavioural dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: The transition from bulk-tissue profiling to single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomics has reshaped our understanding of Alzheimer's disease (AD) from a passive proteinopathy to a coordinated multicellular process spanning the neurovascular unit. Neuronally, selective vulnerability targets projection networks and subclass-specific inhibitory interneurons. Their transcriptional silencing compromises projection pathways, including the entorhinal-hippocampal perforant path, disrupts cortical microcircuits, and underlies episodic memory impairment, hyperexcitability, and executive control failure. This neuronal degeneration is dynamically coupled to reactive glial and vascular remodelling across distinct spatial niches. We examine the non-linear transition of homeostatic astrocytes and microglia into specialized, plaque-associated reactive sub-states, as well as paracrine signalling decay at the neurovascular interface. Compromised capillary tight junctions and the shedding of pericytic survival receptors are proposed to promote blood-brain barrier disintegrity, triggering a feed-forward neuroinflammatory cascade of complement-mediated synaptic pruning. Crucially, we establish a three-tiered hierarchy of evidence, rigorously distinguishing cross-sectional, associative human postmortem findings from inferred functional trajectories in human cellular platforms, and causal, perturbation-based validations in transgenic rodent models. We review how contemporary multi-scale integration-combining single-nucleus transcriptomics with functional electrophysiological platforms and biophysical connectomic modelling-bridges the gap between terminal postmortem signatures and living brain dynamics. Finally, we outline a coordinated translational roadmap illustrating how spatially resolved cell-state networks can guide the development of fluid and imaging biomarkers, support biologically informed patient stratification, enrich clinical trials, and accelerate the development of circuit-restoring precision therapies, thereby providing a mechanistic framework that links cell-state transitions to neural circuit dysfunction, behavioural impairment, and precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: The last gift cohort: advancing HIV reservoir research through single-cell and spatial approaches.
papers.abstract: Purpose of reviewDespite effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), persistent HIV reservoirs remain the primary obstacle to achieving an HIV cure. No single assay, however, establishes proviral intactness, transcriptional activity, cellular identity, spatial position, and neighborhoods at once.SummaryReservoir measurements should be reported by what each assay can establish rather than as interchangeable estimates of reservoir size. Cohorts such as the Last Gift, which yield matched blood and multiorgan tissue from the same donor with longitudinal clinical context, are well suited to applying direct proviral characterization, single-cell phenotyping and spatially resolved viral detection in parallel on the same specimens. This combination defines the resolution - intact provirus, in an identified cell, in a defined tissue niche - that cure trials should increasingly be expected to measure.

papers.title: IER3-N-cadherin axis contributes to apoptosis resistance in dermal fibroblasts under profibrotic conditions
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Persistent activation and resistance to apoptosis of dermal fibroblasts contribute to pathological skin fibrosis. Immediate early response 3 (IER3) is a stress-responsive protein involved in cell survival, but its role in cutaneous fibrosis remains unclear. We investigated the functional significance of IER3 in dermal fibroblasts and its potential contribution to fibrosis. Methods IER3 expression was examined in skin samples from patients with systemic sclerosis, keloids, and hypertrophic scars. Primary human dermal fibroblasts were stimulated with transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1). RNA sequencing, siRNA-mediated gene silencing, quantitative PCR, and flow cytometric apoptosis assays were performed to investigate the downstream mechanisms and functional consequences of IER3 expression. Results IER3 expression was increased in dermal fibroblasts within fibrotic skin lesions and was induced by TGF-β1 independently of SMAD3 and MEK/ERK signaling. Transcriptomic analysis identified CDH2 , encoding N-cadherin, as a downstream target of IER3. Moreover, TGF-β1 induced CDH2 expression in a SMAD3 phosphorylation-dependent manner. IER3 knockdown attenuated TGF-β1-induced CDH2 expression, whereas CDH2 knockdown did not affect IER3 expression. Furthermore, CDH2 knockdown enhanced staurosporine-induced apoptosis in TGF-β1-stimulated fibroblasts, accompanied by a shift in apoptosis-related gene expression toward a pro-apoptotic profile. Conclusion Our findings identify a previously unrecognized IER3-N-cadherin regulatory axis that may promote dermal fibroblast survival by suppressing apoptosis under profibrotic conditions. Targeting this pathway may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for persistent skin fibrosis.

papers.title: Cell state programs offer a potential axis for classifying neuroendocrine tumors.
papers.abstract: Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs) arise from hormone-producing cells in the gut and pancreas. Despite increasing incidence of these tumors, therapeutic options remain limited. Well-differentiated GEP-NETs are classified by anatomic site, morphology, and proliferation indices, but this approach offers limited prognostic resolution among phenotypically similar tumors and constrains personalization of treatment decisions. In this issue of the JCI, Karam, Hoffman, and colleagues profiled 38 pancreatic and small-intestinal NETs using joint single-nucleus RNA and ATAC sequencing and projected the resulting malignant cell-associated programs onto matched spatial transcriptomes. Two conserved malignant states emerged: neuronal-like and secretory neuroendocrine. These states span a continuum in both organ sites, are enriched for largely different transcription factor motifs, and occupy distinct microenvironmental niches. Secretory program scores trended higher in metastatic disease and may carry prognostic value. Taken together, these data describe NET heterogeneity as a cell state axis linked to tissue architecture.

papers.title: SpaceBlocks: an expert-supervised workflow for cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis
papers.abstract: Summary Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has become a central tool in tissue biology, with multiple technologies addressing the issue from a different angle. Each platform imposes its own raw data format conventions, and few workflows address reproducible, scalable, cohort-level analyses while integrating expert-supervised decisions to strengthen computational and biological provenance. In this work, we present SpaceBlocks, a Snakemake workflow for reproducible cohort-level analysis of single-cell resolution-ST data that prioritizes expert supervision over full automation. SpaceBlocks homogenizes heterogeneous platform outputs into a common data format, whose structure is validated to ensure downstream processing. Comprehensive expert supervision is facilitated through per sample quality control and cell type annotation diagnostic visualizations, after which downstream analyses automatically follow. SpaceBlocks also allows the ingestion of technology-agnostic externally formatted data and provides interoperability with existing tools and technologies. We demonstrate the use of SpaceBlocks through the reanalysis of 37 samples from public Visium HD, Xenium 5K and MERSCOPE datasets. SpaceBlocks exhibited processing scalability across the three platforms. This reanalysis identified previously missed cell types in Visium HD and heterogeneous marker gene expression in MERSCOPE, highlighting the need for expert-supervised annotations. Moreover, SpaceBlocks facilitated the identification of differentially expressed genes associated with previously defined multiple sclerosis (MS) spatial domains in MERSCOPE, and transcriptional differences between healthy and malignant colorectal tissues in Visium HD. Together, these findings establish SpaceBlocks as a flexible and reproducible workflow for expert-supervised spatial transcriptomics analysis across technologies and biological cohorts. Availability and Implementation SpaceBlocks is freely available under the MIT license on GitHub https://github.com/cbib/SpaceBlocks and the official Snakemake catalog https://snakemake.github.io/snakemake-workflow-catalog/docs/workflows/cbib/SpaceBlocks.html . SpaceBlocks v0.5.1 code, config files, and the public data formatting scripts used to reproduce the results from this study have been deposited in Zenodo (doi: 10.5281/zenodo.23378236). Contact macha.nikolski@u-bordeaux.fr ; sergiooterino@usal.es Supplementary information Supplementary information is available online. Conflict of interest: None declared.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics decoding of the host response to Klebsiella pneumoniae infection reveals an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis and a spatially organised inflammatory programme
papers.abstract: Background Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp) is a leading cause of hospital and community acquired pneumonia and bacteraemia, and hypervirulent and carbapenem resistant lineages continue to expand worldwide. Although individual omics layers of Kp infection have been profiled, the host-level molecular logic that connects transcriptional, cellular, metabolic and spatial programmes has not been systematically integrated. Methods We curated 16 public datasets spanning four modalities-bulk and dual host pathogen RNA-seq (six datasets; 118 libraries), single-cell RNA-seq (four datasets; ≈164,000 cells), untargeted/targeted metabolomics (four datasets; 1,842 molecular features) and Visium spatial transcriptomics (two datasets; ≈11,400 spots) covering murine lung infection models, hypervirulent and classical Kp strains, carbapenem-resistant isolates and human clinical specimens. Datasets were harmonised through a standardised pipeline (Salmon/DESeq2; Scanpy/Harmony; MetaboAnalyst; RCTD/spacexr), and integrated by WGCNA, GSVA, CellChat, Monocle3, SCENIC, joint-pathway analysis, RCTD deconvolution, and machine-learning feature selection (LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE, XGBoost) with 1,000x bootstrap internal validation and independent external validation. Results Kp infection evoked a coherent 920 gene neutrophil inflammatory response (≈520 up-/≈400 down-regulated genes) dominated by IL-17/TNF/NF-κB signalling, neutrophil degranulation, HIF-1α-linked glycolysis and itaconate biosynthesis. A turquoise co-expression module (r = 0.86 with infection status) yielded a ten-gene hub signature (IRG1, S100A9, IL1B, CXCL2, SLC7A11, HMOX1, PTGS2, NFKBIA, LST1, FCGR3B). Single-cell profiling resolved twelve major lung lineages and eleven myeloid substates, tracing a Monocle3 trajectory from Cxcr2 hi inflammatory neutrophils through an Irg1/Slc7a11 hi oxidative phase into Cxcr4 hi /Trem2 hi suppressive states; CellChat identified S100A8/A9-TLR4 and CXCL2-CXCR2 as the most amplified axes (8.5x and 4.2x). Metabolomics revealed 30-fold pulmonary itaconate accumulation together with succinate and lactate elevation, glucose/glutamine depletion and glutathione collapse, and joint-pathway analysis positioned the TCA-cycle itaconate and ferroptosis modules as the strongest convergent perturbations. Spatial transcriptomics mapped these programmes onto five anatomical niches, with IRG1 expression peaking in the infection core (58% neutrophil content) and declining radially. A ten-gene host-response classification model reached AUC=0.958 in discovery, 0.937 in internal validation and 0.884-0.912 in two independent external cohorts (Brier score 0.071). Conclusions By vertically integrating public multi-omics data, we define an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis that couples inflammatory myeloid expansion to spatially segregated metabolic niches, and we deliver a validated host-side molecular signature that discriminates Kp infection from non-infected states.

papers.title: Autoimmune-shared immune states converge in a CXCL12-CXCR4 fibroblast-immune niche in chronic antibody-mediated rejection.
papers.abstract: Chronic antibody-mediated rejection (CAMR) is a leading cause of late kidney allograft failure and shares features of chronic immune activation with systemic autoimmune diseases, but how circulating immune states connect to spatially organized graft injury and whether related immune features recur in autoimmune inflammation remain unclear. Here, we integrated single-cell profiles from peripheral blood and kidney graft samples from patients with CAMR or stable allograft function and healthy controls with independent transplant cohorts, bulk transcriptomic datasets, spectral flow cytometry, multiplex immunofluorescence, high-resolution spatial transcriptomics, and a large blood immune reference spanning autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. CAMR was associated with reproducible myeloid expansion and enrichment of SLC8A1+ monocytes/macrophages, ANK3+CD4+ memory T cells, ZEB2hi T cells, and CD16+ NK cells. These subsets showed migratory and tissue-interacting transcriptional features, including recurrent CXCR4 and ZEB2 expression, suggesting candidate immune states potentially linked to local graft immune organization. In graft tissue, CXCL12-expressing fibroblasts and CXCR4-expressing immune cells were increased in CAMR. High-resolution spatial transcriptomics localized this fibroblast-immune architecture to perivascular regions marked by endothelial activation and stromal remodeling and placed CAMR-associated immune states within adjacent immune-rich neighborhoods, supporting a CXCL12-CXCR4 axis that may be associated with local immune accumulation. Comparisons with large-scale blood immune reference data and spatial transcriptomic datasets from rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus suggested partial recurrence of related immune states and fibroblast-immune organization. Together, this study links circulating CAMR immune remodeling to a spatially organized CXCL12-CXCR4 fibroblast-immune niche and suggests that elements of this niche recur across alloimmune and autoimmune inflammation.

papers.title: TRACER: twin-contrastive learning for fine-grained and rare spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics.
papers.abstract: MotivationFine-grained and rare spatial domains are difficult to identify in spatial transcriptomics because they contain few spots, show subtle transcriptional differences, and are strongly influenced by neighboring regions.ResultsWe present TRACER, a twin-contrastive learning framework that integrates a graph convolutional autoencoder with neighborhood-aware instance-level and cluster-level contrastive learning. By jointly preserving local spatial continuity and enhancing domain separability, TRACER achieved competitive and generally robust performance compared with representative spatial domain identification methods across multiple spatially resolved transcriptomic datasets, including human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex generated by 10× Visium, mouse brain datasets generated by STARmap, osmFISH, and BARISTAseq, and human breast cancer. TRACER recovered major cortical and anatomical structures, improved the identification of rare or transitional domains in the mouse somatosensory cortex, and revealed candidate functionally distinct small domains within a broadly annotated breast cancer region.Availability and implementationThe source code of TRACER is available at https://github.com/luxin-heart/TRACER.

papers.title: Multiomics Dissection of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer (EOCRC) Reveals an Immunosuppressive Microenvironment and Identifies FAT3 Mutation as a Biomarker of Hot-Like Immune Features.
papers.abstract: Early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC) exhibits distinct clinical and biological features compared with late-onset CRC (LOCRC), yet its genomic architecture and immune microenvironmental determinants remain incompletely characterized. Here, we integrated multiomics discovery analyses of 69 EOCRC and 461 LOCRC patients from the TCGA cohort, complemented by independent validation, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and systems-level network analysis. We identified 10 genes significantly enriched for mutations in EOCRC, including ANXA7, ZNF267, and POLQ, which displayed distinct domain-specific clustering and were validated in an external cohort. Mutational signature decomposition showed that EOCRC was associated with an SBS87-like signature, whereas LOCRC was dominated by SBS1; because TCGA lacks detailed treatment history, this SBS87-like inference should not be interpreted as direct evidence of prior thiopurine exposure. Immunologically, EOCRC displayed an immunosuppressive microenvironment characterized by elevated regulatory T cells, resting NK cells, and tighter immune-stromal coupling, as further supported by spatial transcriptomic analysis. Single-cell atlas analysis identified M2-polarized, SPP1-expressing macrophage subsets in EOCRC. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis identified a mitochondrial-ribosomal biogenesis module as the transcriptional hallmark of EOCRC. Finally, random forest analysis identified FAT3 mutations as a genomic correlate of a hot-like, immune-activated phenotype in EOCRC. Integrative single-cell analysis localized FAT3 predominantly to cancer-associated fibroblasts, especially myofibroblasts, and an in silico FAT3 perturbation analysis suggested potential downstream programs involving extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory signaling, chemokine response, and mitotic spindle regulation. These findings delineate age-stratified genomic and microenvironmental features of EOCRC and generate testable hypotheses for future functional and clinical validation.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics identifies tumor-intrinsic and stromal programs associated with immune exclusion in NSCLC.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has reshaped the treatment of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet durable benefit remains limited to a subset of patients. One major pattern of resistance is immune exclusion, in which CD8+ T cells accumulate in stromal regions but fail to penetrate tumor nests. Here, using discovery and non-overlapping internal validation cohorts of ICB-treated NSCLC patients, we show that spatial CD8+ T-cell exclusion is associated with lower objective response rates and shorter progression-free survival. To characterize the molecular programs linked to this phenotype, we integrated GeoMx spatial transcriptomics, bulk transcriptomic profiling, TCR-probe expression analysis, multiplex immunohistofluorescence, and single-cell spatial neighborhood analyses. Compared with infiltrated tumors, immune-excluded tumors showed reduced expression of genes encoding antigen-presentation machinery in the tumor compartment, including HLA class I genes and TAP1, with an altered relationship between IFN-γ-associated transcriptional signals and expression of antigen-presentation machinery. At the stromal level, excluded tumors were enriched for myofibroblastic cancer-associated fibroblast programs and peri-epithelial collagen-rich architecture, whereas infiltrated tumors displayed immune-supportive stromal signatures. CD8-enriched regions from excluded tumors showed reduced metabolic activation and lower TCR-probe expression diversity, without a marked increase in canonical exhaustion markers. These findings provide an integrated, compartment-resolved description of tumor-intrinsic and stromal features associated with immune exclusion in NSCLC and support further evaluation of spatial immune contexture as a complementary biomarker in ICB-treated patients.

papers.title: An Observational Study of Programmed Cell Death In Hypertrophic Scars and Keloids Based on Bibliometric Analysis.
papers.abstract: Hypertrophic scars (HS) and keloids are fibroproliferative disorders caused by abnormal wound healing. Their features include excessive fibroblast proliferation, extracellular matrix deposition, and persistent inflammation. Programmed cell death (PCD) is known to be involved in these conditions, but the current state of PCD pathways studied in HS and keloids has not yet been reviewed. This study used bibliometric analysis to describe the current state of PCD research in HS and keloids, to identify the hotspots and trends. The authors retrieved publications on PCD in HS and keloids from the Web of Science Core Collection. For the bibliometric analysis, the authors used VOSviewer (version 1.6.21). A total of 312 articles were included in this study. In the coauthorship analysis of countries, China, the United States, and Germany formed a core triangle in the field. In the coauthorship analysis of organizations, Shanghai Jiao Tong University showed the highest strength. The most productive institution, journal, and author were Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Wound Repair and Regeneration, and Long Xiao, respectively. In the cocited analysis, the foundational authors were Desmoulière A, Ladin Daniel A, and Sayah DN; the foundational journals were the Journal of Investigative Dermatology and Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery. The keyword co-occurrence map revealed that the most active research topics were "apoptosis," "ferroptosis," "autophagy," and "noncoding RNAs," and the overlay map indicated that the most recent hotspots were "ferroptosis" and "autophagy." Four principal research hotspots emerged from the analysis: apoptosis, ferroptosis, autophagy, and noncoding RNAs. Ferroptosis and autophagy may emerge as future research trends.Level of evidenceLevel III.

papers.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts: origins, functional heterogeneity and therapeutic potential.
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are integral components of the tumor microenvironment (TME) and are increasingly recognized as critical regulators of nearly every hallmark of cancer. Once viewed as a uniform, protumorigenic cell type, it is now clear that CAFs comprise a spectrum of dynamic and plastic functional states with both tumor-promoting and tumor-restraining capacities. This functional duality, conceptualized within the framework of cancer as a "wound that fails to heal", is dictated by their diverse cellular origins, the specific activation pathways engaged (such as TGF-β and PDGF), and the evolving cues from the TME. In this Review, we dissect the multifaceted roles of CAFs, from their promotion of cancer cell proliferation, invasion and angiogenesis through secreted factors and extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, to their profound influence on the immune landscape. We detail how distinct CAF subsets, such as myofibroblastic (myCAFs) and inflammatory (iCAFs) CAFs, orchestrate an immunosuppressive niche and contribute to therapeutic resistance. We also explore the compelling evidence for tumor-suppressive CAF functions, which have catalyzed a paradigm shift in therapeutic strategies-moving away from indiscriminate CAF ablation towards nuanced approaches aimed at reprogramming their state. These strategies include modulating key signaling pathways, normalizing the CAF-remodeled ECM, and exploiting unique metabolic vulnerabilities. Finally, we discuss how advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are resolving this complexity, paving the way for the development of precision therapies that can selectively neutralize pro-tumorigenic CAF activities while harnessing their beneficial functions to improve patient outcomes.

papers.title: Identification of ageing-related genes in prostate cancer with type 2 Diabetes using machine learning: a multi-omics study focusing on SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) demonstrates complex associations with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and ageing, though their interconnected molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. This study aimed to identify and validate diagnostic biomarkers at the intersection of these pathways to enable early detection and risk stratification in high-risk populations. Bioinformatic analysis was performed on PCa and T2DM transcriptomic data downloaded from the GEO database, followed by differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and functional enrichment. Eight machine learning algorithms were applied to identify hub ageing-related genes (ARGs), with SHAP analysis interpreting feature importance. A nomogram model was constructed and validated across multiple cohorts. Immune infiltration, drug sensitivity, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics were used for mechanistic exploration. Three key ARGs (SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4) were identified and used to develop a diagnostic model with high accuracy (AUCs: 0.726-0.905). SOX4 promoted immune evasion, PRNP exhibited context-dependent duality, and FOXO4 functioned as a tumor suppressor. Spatial and single-cell analyses revealed cell-type-specific expression and fibroblast-epithelial communication via MIF, LRP1, and FZD1. Drug sensitivity profiling identified abiraterone and docetaxel as potential therapeutics for high- and low-risk patients, respectively. In conclusion, SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4 are key biomarkers linking PCa, T2DM, and ageing, and the diagnostic model shows robust performance and clinical utility, providing insights into microenvironment-driven mechanisms and personalized treatment strategies for PCa patients with T2DM.

papers.title: Myeloid Suppressor Cells Drive HCC Invasiveness via the THBS1-SDC4 Pathway.
papers.abstract: Background & aimsMonocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) accumulate in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but their activation and tumor-promoting mechanisms remain unclear. We investigated how stromal-myeloid-tumor crosstalk promotes HCC invasiveness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT).MethodsWe analyzed single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 36 HCC patients and spatial transcriptomics data from 2 HCC specimens to characterize M-MDSC localization and intercellular signaling. Matrix cancer-associated fibroblast and M-MDSC phenotypes and interactions were assessed using molecular and functional assays. Thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling was investigated in xenografts in immunodeficient mice (n = 8/group) and diethylnitrosamine/carbon tetrachloride-induced HCC in the immunocompetent mice (n = 6/group).ResultsM-MDSCs preferentially localized to EMT-active tumor margins and correlated with EMT activity (Spearman r = 0.30; false discovery rate = 3.3 × 10-4) and shorter overall survival (log-rank P = 0.00124). Matrix cancer-associated fibroblasts promoted M-MDSC activation through collagen-associated CD44 signaling. Activated M-MDSCs induced EMT through thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling, whereas syndecan-4 deficiency suppressed tumor cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and EMT. Thrombospondin-1-deficient M-MDSCs reduced xenograft progression and increased interferon-γ-positive CD8+ T-cell infiltration and cytotoxic immune markers in immunocompetent HCC. A thrombospondin communication pathway score was associated with shorter overall survival (log-rank P = 2.28 × 10-5; Cox hazard ratio = 1.23, P = 0.0193).ConclusionsMatrix cancer-associated fibroblasts promote monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cell activation, driving epithelial-mesenchymal transition in hepatocellular carcinoma through thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling. Targeting this axis may restrain tumor progression and enhance antitumor immunity.Impact and implicationsThis study provides mechanistic insight into how M-MDSCs are activated within the HCC tumor microenvironment and subsequently drive tumor cell EMT through THBS1-SDC4 signaling. These findings highlight the importance of tumor-immune-stromal crosstalk in HCC progression and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding the pro-tumor functions of M-MDSCs. The THBS1-SDC4 axis may represent a therapeutically targetable pathway to restrain M-MDSC-mediated tumor aggressiveness and modulate the tumor microenvironment. Further validation in independent clinical cohorts and assessment of therapeutic efficacy are warranted to determine its translational potential.

papers.title: Single-cell landscape of human adipose tissue reveals THBS1 as a potential driver of fibro-inflammation in metabolic disease.
papers.abstract: The cellular complexity of adipose tissue plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of metabolic disease; however, mechanisms underlying adipose dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we constructed a single-nucleus and bulk transcriptomic atlas of human visceral adipose tissues from an ethnically homogeneous cohort with defined metabolic states: lean with normal glucose tolerance, obesity, and obesity with type 2 diabetes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed a fibro-inflammatory subpopulation of adipose stem cells and adipocytes characterized by high THBS1 expression, which were enriched in individuals with obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes compared to lean controls. Through complementary in vitro (human primary ASCs, THP-1 macrophages, and Matrigel-captured mature adipocytes), ex vivo (mouse and human visceral adipose tissue explants), and in vivo (gain-of-function and antibody-mediated neutralization) experiments, we demonstrated that THBS1 promoted adipose fibrosis and inflammation via macrophage-mediated TGFβ activation, impairing adipogenesis and adipocyte function. Inhibition of THBS1 attenuated fibro-inflammatory features in metabolically dysfunctional adipose tissues. Moreover, THBS1 levels in plasma and adipocytes correlated with metabolic traits, including BMI and HbA1c. Collectively, our study provides a cellular atlas of human visceral adipose tissues across metabolic disease states and identifies THBS1 as a key pathogenic driver and potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics.
papers.abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.

papers.title: Standardizing spatial transcriptomic analysis for infectious diseases with STID.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomic studies of infectious diseases still rely on fragmented data analysis processes. Here, we developed STID (spatial transcriptomics toolkit for infectious diseases), a standardized framework for spatial transcriptomic analysis of infectious diseases that leverages the Seurat ecosystem and incorporates Python-based modules. STID provides an extensible infection-specific data structure and supports a full suite of analyses, such as pathogen background correction, infection-associated spot and niche identification, single-sample niche characterization, and multi-sample comparative and temporal analyses. STID is broadly applicable to spatial transcriptomic data from infectious diseases caused by bacteria, viruses, and parasites and enables systematic characterization of the structural features, cellular composition, molecular functions, and host-pathogen interactions within pathogen-infected and/or host-responsive niches. Overall, STID provides an accessible, reproducible, and extensible framework for analyzing infection-associated spatial transcriptomic data and for dissecting host-pathogen interactions in their native spatial microenvironments.

papers.title: Nano-kinetic implant surface mediates osteo-antibacterial synergy through electromagnetic-mechanical coupling.
papers.abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication of total joint arthroplasty, mainly caused by bacterial biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance. Traditional static surfaces rely on contact killing-based bactericidal properties and cannot reliably clear mature biofilms. In this study, we fabricate a remote-activated dynamic biomimetic system, namely a movable magnetic topographic surface (MMTS). Here we show that under the exposure of external electromagnetic field (EMF), the anchored Janus nano-heterodimers oscillate periodically to mechanically disrupt bacterial membranes and eradicates biofilms of Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. This mechanical force can also activates Piezo1 mechanosensitive ion channel in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), inducing calcium oscillations, upregulating gene expression of Runx2 and BMP2, and enhancing extracellular matrix mineralization. In vivo, MMTS combined with EMF exposure eliminates local infection and promoted osseointegration. This remote-activated dynamic biomimetic strategy offers a promising multifunctional platform for PJI treatment, and improved implant osteointegration in clinical orthopedics.
