papers.title: Multi-omics, spatial omics and artificial intelligence in chronic diseases: current applications and future directions.
papers.abstract: Chronic diseases exhibit multiscale heterogeneity and spatial organization, yet analytical frameworks often fail to connect molecular perturbations, tissue architecture, and clinical outcomes within a unified evidence framework. Bulk and single-modality approaches can identify regulatory or cellular alterations but provide limited insight into why pathogenic programs emerge in anatomical regions, how they shape disease niches, and how they drive divergent clinical trajectories. Multi-omics partially addresses this gap by resolving interconnected layers of regulation, transcription, protein activity, and metabolism, whereas spatial omics maps these processes within preserved tissue architecture, enabling the delineation of lesion topology, interface states, and multicellular microenvironments. Artificial intelligence (AI) may further extend this framework by integrating molecular, spatial, imaging, and clinical data into disease representations that support disease stratification, the discovery of mechanistic patterns, and clinically testable predictions, provided that models are externally validated, biologically interpretable, and robust to dataset bias and domain shift. In this review, we examine how multi-omics, spatial omics, and AI can bridge the disconnect between molecular profiling, spatial pathology, and clinical translation in chronic disease research. We discuss six representative disease domains before synthesizing insights into how these approaches define molecular endotypes, map pathological niches, identify recurrent mechanistic patterns, and generate interpretable surrogate readouts for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment stratification. We also highlight limitations, including preanalytical variability, inconsistencies across platforms, limited external generalizability, and the challenges of translating high-dimensional outputs into deployable clinical tools. Finally, we outline priorities for scalable evidence systems, mechanism-guided validation frameworks, multimodal model interpretability, and prospective clinical implementation.

papers.title: Regenerative agents versus autogenous bone graft for alveolar cleft reconstruction: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutogenous iliac crest bone graft is the standard for alveolar cleft reconstruction, but donor-site morbidity has prompted interest in regenerative agents. This review compared and ranked these agents against autogenous bone and one another.MethodsFollowing the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for network meta-analyses, six databases were searched from January 2000 to June 2026 for controlled studies comparing a regenerative agent with autogenous bone graft. Risk of bias was assessed using version 2 of the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials and the ROBINS-I tool; certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. A frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis used autogenous bone as the reference and P-scores to rank treatments for new bone formation, bone density, graft volume, and graft success.ResultsTwenty-one studies (23 reports) were included. Platelet-rich fibrin (risk ratio [RR], 1.46; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.07-2.01) and concentrated growth factor (RR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.02-1.43) were superior to autograft for graft success; platelet-rich fibrin ranked first (P-score, 0.87) and exceeded recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (RR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.04-1.99). In one trial, bone marrow aspirate concentrate increased graft volume (standardized mean difference, 2.36; 95% CI, 1.51-3.21). No agent increased new bone formation or bone density. Certainty was moderate for one comparison, low for six, and very low for nine.ConclusionAutogenous bone remains the volumetric reference standard. The improvement in graft success with platelet-rich fibrin was supported by moderate-certainty evidence and persisted across all sensitivity analyses, including restriction to randomized evidence. The concentrated growth factor finding had low certainty, relied on one retrospective study, and did not persist when analyses were restricted to radiographic outcomes. Adequately powered randomized trials with standardized methods are needed.

papers.title: Metabolite-Driven Immunometabolic Crosstalk in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: The Macrophage-Disc Cell Interface.
papers.abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) is accompanied by extracellular-matrix disruption, metabolic stress and immune-cell infiltration, but how metabolites mediate communication between disc cells and macrophages remains incompletely defined. This narrative review examines lactate, succinate and kynurenine as candidate signalling metabolites at the macrophage-disc cell interface and proposes an integrative metabolite-centred framework. Evidence is strongest for lactate, which is supported by IVDD-specific studies linking glycolytic adaptation and impaired clearance to acidosis, MCT-dependent metabolic coupling, ASIC/NLRP3 activation, lactylation, cellular senescence and matrix catabolism. Evidence for succinate is more limited: IVDD-specific studies support SIRT5-AIFM1-dependent succinylation and mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas succinate accumulation and SUCNR1-mediated macrophage signalling in human degenerative discs remain unverified. The kynurenine-AhR axis is primarily hypothesis-generating; emerging IVDD-related observations implicate AhR and tryptophan-pathway changes, but a causal kynurenine-AhR macrophage-disc pathway has not been established. We propose that degenerating disc cells may reprogramme the local metabolic microenvironment, thereby altering macrophage functional states and creating a self-amplifying immunometabolic loop that feeds back on disc-cell injury and extracellular-matrix degradation. Future studies should combine spatial immunometabolomics in human tissue with cell-specific and causal intervention experiments to distinguish established mechanisms from context-dependent or extrapolated pathways and to evaluate potential microenvironment-directed therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Extracellular Vesicles in Periodontitis: Bidirectional Crosstalk Between Periodontal Inflammation and Systemic Diseases.
papers.abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that leads to the destruction of tooth supporting tissues, including gingival inflammation, periodontal attachment loss, and alveolar bone resorption. Increasing evidence suggests that periodontitis also increases susceptibility to a range of systemic conditions and there is a reciprocal communication between the periodontum and systemic organs. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), as key mediators of intercellular communication, can transport proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids across biological barriers and may play an important role in this crosstalk. In this review, we synthesize current evidence for the involvement of EVs in communication between periodontitis and distant organs. Compared with previous reviews that mainly focus on Porphyromonas gingivalis EVs or one-way effects, we synthesize evidence across multiple EV sources (bacterial, host periodontal, and circulating biofluid EVs) and explicitly review both directions of signaling. At present, the evidence is considerably stronger for periodontal-to-systemic EV effects, particularly in endothelial dysfunction, metabolic reprogramming, osteoclastogenic signaling, and barrier disruption in distant organs, whereas the evidence of systemic EVs on periodontitis remains limited, fragmented, and largely preclinical. This marked imbalance identifies the systemic-to-oral EV pathway as a major knowledge gap in the field. Further studies are needed to define the sources, cargoes, and functional significance of EVs in oral-systemic crosstalk and to clarify their translational potential as biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Condylectomy for active unilateral condylar hyperplasia: a single-arm meta-analysis of secondary orthognathic surgery and demographic outcomes.
papers.abstract: The objective was to quantify the proportion of patients requiring secondary orthognathic surgery after condylectomy for active unilateral condylar hyperplasia (UCH) and to assess whether outcomes differ among high, proportional, and adaptable condylectomy techniques. Secondary aims were to pool sex distribution and age at surgery. A systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis were conducted according to PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched up to 31 October 2025. Eligible studies reported outcomes of condylectomy for active UCH with ≥3 patients and ≥12 months of follow-up. Female proportion and mean age were pooled respectively. Seventeen studies, including 476 patients, were analyzed. The pooled random-effects estimate for secondary orthognathic surgery was 15.4% (95% confidence interval (CI) 4.7-29.7%). Subgroup analysis showed no significant difference among high, proportional, and adaptable condylectomy (P = 0.41). The pooled proportion of female patients was 63% (95% CI 56-70%; I2 = 40.3%) and the pooled mean age at surgery was 23.47 years; however, very high heterogeneity limits the interpretability of a single summary estimate, and the observed age range may be more informative clinically (95% CI 19.72-27.22; I2 = 89.6%). No condylectomy variant demonstrated statistically detectable differences in orthognathic surgery rates. Patients are predominantly young adult females. Condylectomy should be considered a central component of early management of active UCH, although further standardized prospective studies are needed.

papers.title: Extracellular matrix ageing as a biological variable in 3D cancer models: A framework for age-aware model design.
papers.abstract: Ageing is a major determinant of cancer risk and outcome, yet age-associated changes in the extracellular matrix (ECM) remain poorly represented in most preclinical cancer models. Throughout life, the ECM undergoes alterations in composition, architecture, biochemical modification, mechanics and turnover that influence cell behaviour and tissue function. Although advanced three-dimensional (3D) cancer models increasingly incorporate ECM components, ageing is rarely considered as an independent biological variable, and the terms aged, ageing-associated and age-mimetic ECM are often applied to biologically distinct experimental systems. Here, we review current evidence describing ECM remodelling across the lifespan and evaluate how age-associated matrix states have been incorporated into 3D cancer models. We propose a framework that distinguishes four principal modelling strategies: chronologically aged ECM models, defined age-associated ECM modification models, cell-mediated ECM remodelling models, and mixed multicomponent ageing models. These approaches differ substantially in the ageing-associated features they reproduce, the degree of biological fidelity they provide and the strength of mechanistic inference they permit. Analysis of published studies provides evidence that age-associated ECM states can influence tumour invasion, proliferation, signalling and therapeutic response across many cancer types. At the same time, the available evidence indicates that ECM ageing is a multidimensional process that no single molecular or mechanical surrogate can capture. Hence, we argue that age-aware cancer models should be classified and interpreted according to the specific ageing-associated ECM features they reproduce and experimentally validate. By establishing ECM ageing as a definable biological variable, this framework provides practical guidance for designing, validating, and interpreting next-generation age-aware 3D in vitro cancer models.

papers.title: Mechanistic study of ECM phenotype switch in epicardial adipose tissue in atrial fibrillation: A bioinformatics study.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common cardiac arrhythmia. Differential expression analysis identified 610 differentially expressed genes. Notably, the basement membrane-specific collagen COL4A4 was significantly upregulated in AF (log2FC = 4.37, Padj = 2.7 × 10-9), accompanied by significant upregulation of COL4A3, whereas interstitial collagen repair genes (COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, and FN1) showed consistent downregulation, defining an "ECM phenotype switch" characterized by suppressed interstitial repair coupled with independent basement membrane deposition; the fibrinolysis inhibitor SERPINE1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1) was also markedly upregulated (log2FC = 3.89, Padj = .026). Gene set enrichment analysis implicated ribosome biogenesis and translation dysregulation as a potential associated upstream program (normalized enrichment score = 2.26-3.03 and false discovery rate = 0.012-0.013). AF-related EAT exhibits an ECM phenotype switch characterized by suppressed interstitial collagen repair and independent basement membrane collagen deposition, potentially associated with ribosome biogenesis dysregulation. These hypothesis-generating findings provide a novel framework for understanding EAT-mediated atrial remodeling in AF.

papers.title: Electrochemical interactions in the oral cavity: The clinical significance of oral galvanism - a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Electrochemical reactions in the oral cavity, caused by small-scale electric charges between different metallic prosthetic materials, are often overlooked in modern dentistry. Although multiple metallic alloys are frequently used in dentistry, their unintentional interactions may lead to both localized tissue effects and have been hypothesized to contribute to broader biological consequences. However, awareness of these interactions remains insufficient among dental practitioners and patients. A narrative review of the literature was conducted using electronic databases including PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and Embase. Relevant studies addressing the etiology, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, prevention, and management of oral galvanism were identified and qualitatively synthesized. The reviewed literature indicates that electrochemical interactions between metallic dental materials can result in galvanic current generation, corrosion processes, metal ion release, and a variety of oral manifestations. Previous reports have suggested that more than 30 different metallic components may coexist within a single oral cavity, highlighting the complexity of oral electrochemical interactions. While several studies have proposed potential associations with broader biological and systemic effects, the available evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Recognizing the effects of electrochemical activity in the oral cavity is essential for enhancing biocompatibility, ensuring patient safety, and improving the longevity of dental restorations. This review seeks to address existing knowledge gaps and promote further research into this often-overlooked aspect of dental health.

papers.title: A biological approach for corticoperiosteal free flaps in mandibular reconstruction without rigid fixation: the wrapping technique.
papers.abstract: Mandibular reconstruction in irradiated or otherwise compromised bone environments requires both mechanical stability and biological revitalization of devitalized tissue. Corticoperiosteal flaps from the medial femoral condyle provide a thin, vascularized osteogenic interface particularly suited to restoring bone vitality in limited mandibular defects, but their effectiveness depends on stable fixation and intimate periosteal contact, both of which may be compromised by postoperative edema or the use of rigid hardware. The vascularized periosteum is then drawn around the superior mandibular margin and secured to create a watertight biological envelope. This approach aims to optimize osseous integration, reduce hardware-related complications, and enhance revascularization in irradiated, infected, or osteonecrotic bone. The technique may be particularly relevant in non-interruptive oncologic mandibulectomies requiring postoperative radiotherapy and may be extended to other periosteal flaps for small or localized mandibular defects. This hardware-free, biologically oriented method provides a simple and effective option for selected mandibular reconstructions.

papers.title: smoothclust: Spatial smoothing and boundary-density summaries for spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables the measurement of gene expression while preserving tissue organization. A common analysis task is the identification of spatial domains, defined here as spatially coherent regions with consistent expression profiles or cell-type mixtures and represented using categorical spatial tissue maps. However, while numerous methods have been developed to identify spatial domains, interpretable summary measures to quantify spatial domain organization and tissue architecture at the sample level remain less standardized. Here, we present smoothclust, a framework for spatial domain analysis consisting of two components: a spatial-smoothing-based clustering workflow for generating spatial domain labels, and a boundary density (BD) metric that provides local and sample-level summaries of label transitions on a spatial graph. Building on established categorical spatial statistics, the raw BD metric is calculated from the proportion of neighboring spatial locations that are assigned to different domain labels, and requires only spatial coordinates and domain labels as inputs. The metric can be calculated using either our spatial-smoothing-based domain labels or labels from external clustering methods or manual annotations. Relative BD is a composition-adjusted summary, calculated by dividing raw BD by its expectation under random relabeling with the observed label counts. By quantifying label transitions, our framework translates spatial domain label maps into interpretable local and sample-level summary measures of tissue architecture, facilitating exploratory analyses and comparisons across samples and biological conditions. We demonstrate the approach through evaluations across datasets from several spatial transcriptomics platforms and simulations. The spatial-smoothing workflow and BD metric are implemented in the smoothclust R package, which is freely available from Bioconductor and GitHub.

papers.title: Glycolysis in pulmonary fibrosis: From drivers to therapeutic opportunities (Review).
papers.abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is a chronic and progressive interstitial lung disease with a poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Current antifibrotic therapies only slow disease progression, underscoring an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. In recent years, metabolic reprogramming, notably the shift towards aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect), has emerged as a key driver of PF pathogenesis. This review comprehensively examines the central role of glycolysis in fueling the fibrotic cascade. It summarizes the major risk factors and fundamental pathogenic mechanisms of PF. The review then delves into the molecular mechanisms by which profibrotic signals, such as TGF‑β1, remodel cellular metabolism. The upregulation and pathogenic roles of critical glycolytic nodes are detailed‑including glucose transporters, hexokinase 2, phosphofructokinase‑2/fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphatase 3, pyruvate kinase M2 and lactate dehydrogenase A‑in activated fibroblasts, injured epithelial cells and pro‑fibrotic immune cells. Furthermore, the interplay between glycolysis and key signaling pathways (TGF‑β1, hypoxia‑inducible factor‑1α, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Hippo, AMP‑activated protein kinase and sirtuins) that form feed‑forward loops to sustain the fibrotic process is discussed. Furthermore, therapeutic strategies targeting glycolytic enzymes and upstream metabolic checkpoints are highlighted, summarizing preclinical evidence for small‑molecule inhibitors and non‑coding RNAs as emerging regulators of glycolytic reprogramming. By consolidating current knowledge on glycolysis‑centric metabolic underpinnings of PF, this review underscores the promise of metabolism‑based interventions and discusses challenges for translating these findings into effective therapies.

papers.title: Defining Osseointegration for Biodegradable Scaffolds based on Histological, Immunohistochemical and Ultrastructural Analysis.
papers.abstract: Osseointegration of metal implants refers to the formation of a direct, intimate, and stable interface between bone and the implant surface under physiological loads, without intervening fibrous tissue. This concept is largely based on the long-term fixation of non-degradable implants, where bone remodeling occurs around a permanent material. However, there is no equivalent framework defining de biological integration of biodegradable scaffolds used for scaffold-guided bone regeneration (SGBR), whose architecture, mechanical properties, and surface chemistry are intentionally desined to change over time. Consequently, definitions developed for permanent mettalic are frequently applied to biodegradable scaffolds, leading to uncertainty regarding whether these scaffolds truly "osseointegrate". We argue that the biological processes at biodegradable scaffold-bone interfaces fundamentally differs from that of metallic implants, and should be distinguished. Rather than classical "bone anchorage", biodegradable scaffolds support a dynamic, immunologically active, and mechanically evolving bone-scaffold interface in which fibrous encapsulation and bone formation compete. This paper aims to clarify these issues not by redefining osseointegration in general, but by adapting it specifically to osteoconductive biodegradable scaffolds in SGBR. Using evidence from a series of studies in well-characterised large-animal models of segmental bone defects, we propose a new framework that captures the temporal, cellular, and structural complexities of osseointegration of biodegradable scaffolds in living organisms. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Biodegradable scaffolds are intended to facilitate bone regeneration and gradually degrade as new tissue develops. Nevertheless, there is limited knowledge about how these materials interact with bone over extended periods. This research examines the bone-scaffold interface over 36-months using histology, immunohistochemistry, scanning electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy. Results indicate that biodegradable scaffolds do not form the permanent bonds commonly defined as osseointegration in metallic implants. Instead, they establish a dynamic interface that evolves as the organ bone, composed of mineralised tissue, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix, remodels around the degrading scaffold. These insights improve our understanding of scaffold-guided bone regeneration and will guide the development of next-generation biodegradable scaffolds that shorten the timeframe and better support long-term bone growth.

Future translation will require longitudinal, spatially resolved and clinically anchored integration to support risk stratification, at-risk metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis detection, fibrosis assessment, treatment-response prediction and precision medicine in MASLD.

papers.title: Toward a digital urinary biopsy for early risk stratification in diabetic kidney disease: Anchoring shed cells, vesicles, and cell-free DNA to spatial kidney cell states.
papers.abstract: BackgroundDiabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide. However, albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which define and stage DKD, report established injury and do not resolve the cellular heterogeneity underlying variable progression. For each compartment, we tabulate study population, sample size, processing, assay, performance and validation status. Because shed-cell RNA, selectively sorted vesicle cargo and cfDNA methylation differ in origin, measurement scale and bias, each requires its own reference matrix, sampling function and background terms. All three carry renal information in feasibility studies, yet none is a validated clinical assay in DKD. Moreover, a cfDNA methylation reference at the required resolution is lacking, and no named computational method has been tested on urine.ConclusionWe therefore present the framework as a structured research hypothesis and define the required validation, from analytical and clinical validity to prospective demonstration of utility, with non-albuminuric DKD, which albuminuria-based screening misses, as the index use case. It offers a testable route to cell-resolved, non-invasive staging of DKD rather than a demonstrated capability.

papers.title: GeneCMamba: Autoregressive spatial transcriptome prediction from histopathology via state-space sequence modeling and adaptive cross-modal gating.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics provides spatially resolved molecular profiles but remains constrained by cost, throughput, and technical variability. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) images offers a scalable alternative, although cross-modal alignment remains challenging because morphology and transcription are probabilistically related and represented at different scales. We propose GeneCMamba, a contrastive learning-guided generative framework that formulates spatial gene expression prediction as autoregressive gene-token generation. A dual-encoder architecture first aligns histopathological and transcriptomic representations in a shared latent space. A state-space model decoder then captures long-range dependencies among gene tokens with linear computational complexity, while a cross-modal gating mechanism uses gene queries to retain informative morphological features and suppress staining artifacts and irrelevant background. Experiments on six tissue datasets comprising approximately 23,500 spatial samples showed that GeneCMamba outperformed all evaluated baselines. On the breast dataset, it achieved a token accuracy of 82.42% and an F1 score of 0.78 and converged five epochs earlier than the comparison models. Ablation studies confirmed the complementary contributions of the decoder and gating mechanism. Moreover, spatial reconstruction of FN1 reproduced heterogeneous expression patterns in stroma-rich regions, supporting the biological relevance of the predictions. GeneCMamba therefore provides an efficient framework for inferring spatial molecular profiles from routine histopathology images.

papers.title: Research progress on the effects of implant-supported overdentures on residual ridge remodelling in edentulous jaws: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Residual ridge resorption (RRR) following tooth loss is a continuous and irreversible process that limits the effectiveness of conventional complete dentures and compromises masticatory function and quality of life. Implant-supported overdentures (implant overdentures [IODs]) can reconstruct physiological stress distribution, regulate inflammatory molecular signalling and optimise bone remodelling through combined biological and mechanical pathways, thereby helping to slow RRR. This review systematically summarises the biological mechanisms of RRR, including inflammatory mediators, the receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand/osteoprotegerin pathway and systemic factors; the mechanical mechanisms, including Wolff's law and stress distribution patterns; the protective effects of IODs on residual ridges; key determinants of their bone-preserving efficacy, including implant-, attachment-, occlusion- and patient-related factors; current controversies; and advances in digital applications. Regarding attachment systems, current evidence from randomised controlled trials, long-term cohort studies and meta-analyses indicates that ball, Locator and bar attachments demonstrate broadly comparable peri-implant marginal bone outcomes, although Locator attachments may be associated with lower posterior RRR over 10 years, whereas bar attachments may offer superior crestal bone stability in specific clinical scenarios. No single attachment system demonstrates a clinically meaningful, reproducible advantage in bone preservation, and selection should be individualised based on anatomical, functional and maintenance considerations. Current evidence remains limited by heterogeneous study designs, variable follow-up periods and an overreliance on finite element analyses, underscoring the need for standardised long-term clinical trials with harmonised outcome measures. Evidence from recent high-quality studies over the past 5 years is integrated to propose stratified clinical recommendations according to bone volume, systemic status and economic factors. Digital technologies, including computer-guided surgery, digital impressions and occlusal analysis, further enhance precision and predictability of bone-preserving outcomes. This review provides a theoretical basis and clinical reference for optimising rehabilitation protocols, preserving residual ridges over the long term and improving prosthetic prognosis in patients with edentulism.

papers.title: Clinical outcomes of a novel one-piece niobia-modified zirconia implant compared with a titanium implant at 48 weeks: a multicenter randomized controlled trial.

papers.title: CATFISHR: integration of transcriptome and inferred CNV profiles for comprehensive malignant cell identification
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Malignant cell identification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) remains challenging because transcriptomic cell typing, somatic variant detection and inferred copy-number approaches each have modality-specific limitations. Rare or ambiguous malignant populations are especially vulnerable to misclassification or exclusion, despite their relevance to treatment resistance, minimal residual disease, and metastasis. We developed CATFISHR, a semi-automated workflow that integrates RNA-expression similarity, inferred copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and consensus cell typing to classify malignant cells relative to high-confidence references. CATFISHR was evaluated across eight cohorts, including seven scRNA-seq datasets spanning multiple carcinomas and melanoma subtypes, and one 10x Visium spatial transcriptomics sample. Compared with available benchmarks or ground truths, CATFISHR achieved balanced accuracy > 0.85 in six of eight cohorts and F1 score > 0.80 in six of eight cohorts. Cells uniquely identified by CATFISHR as malignant (“Hidden” cells) were present in every dataset and were not consistently explained by standard quality-control metrics. In several cohorts, Hidden cells were transcriptionally closer to benchmark malignant than non-malignant compartments; in Visium data, sampled Hidden spots contained histologist-confirmed morphologically malignant cells. CATFISHR reduces missed malignant calls while preserving rare, transitional and benchmark-discordant populations for downstream investigation. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT

papers.title: Genetic axes of hand and shoulder soft-tissue disease and their divergent responses to adiposity and incretin therapy: a cross-biobank genomic and randomised trial study
papers.abstract: BackgroundHand and shoulder soft-tissue disorders cluster in people with obesity and diabetes, now widely treated with incretin receptor agonists. Whether these disorders share genetic causes, and whether pharmacological weight loss relieves or provokes them, is unknown. MethodsWe analysed genome-wide data on seven disorders from FinnGen and UK Biobank (over 900,000 participants) by genomic structural equation modelling, tested five endocrine and metabolic exposures by Mendelian randomisation, mapped heritability onto 110,020 connective-tissue cells, and pooled serious adverse events from 210 placebo-controlled trials of incretin receptor agonists (134,138 participants). Each SD higher genetically predicted body mass index increased the odds of carpal tunnel syndrome (odds ratio [OR] 1{middle dot}67, 95% CI 1{middle dot}47-1{middle dot}89; P = 6{middle dot}9 x 10-16) and decreased those of Dupuytrens disease (0{middle dot}57, 0{middle dot}46-0{middle dot}71; P = 8{middle dot}7 x 10-7), whose heritability concentrated in lesional POSTN+ fibroblasts. Incretin receptor agonists increased serious fibro-capsular events (Peto OR 3{middle dot}88, 1{middle dot}83-8{middle dot}25; P = 4{middle dot}1 x 10-4), including frozen shoulder (4{middle dot}16, 1{middle dot}50-11{middle dot}54) and Dupuytrens disease (3{middle dot}58, 1{middle dot}17-10{middle dot}93), but not tenosynovial events (1{middle dot}02, 0{middle dot}60-1{middle dot}75). InterpretationHand and shoulder soft-tissue disease comprises two genetically distinct axes with opposite responses to adiposity. It identifies frozen shoulder and Dupuytrens disease as musculoskeletal pharmacovigilance targets for the millions receiving incretin receptor agonists. FundingHealth Commission of Hubei Province (WJ2023F086) and Department of Science and Technology of Hubei Province (2024BCB059). Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed from database inception to 26 October 2026, without language restrictions, for studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, trigger finger, de Quervain tenosynovitis, Dupuytrens disease, frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis), plantar fasciitis or plantar fibromatosis combined with the terms "genome-wide association", "Mendelian randomisation", "genetic correlation" or "shared genetic", or with glucagon-like peptide-1 or incretin receptor agonists (including semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide and exenatide). We also searched the GWAS Catalog for summary statistics of these disorders and the ClinicalTrials.gov results database for placebo-controlled trials of incretin receptor agonists. The searches returned 131 records on genome-wide association, 73 on Mendelian randomisation, 13 on genetic correlation or shared genetics and 23 on incretin drugs. Genome-wide studies had examined these disorders one at a time or in pairs, and had found shared genetic risk between trigger finger and carpal tunnel syndrome, between frozen shoulder and Dupuytrens disease, and between Dupuytrens disease and body mass index. Mendelian randomisation studies, mostly in UK Biobank, had reported that adiposity, glycaemia and IGF-1 increase the risk of carpal tunnel syndrome and that adiposity decreases that of Dupuytrens disease, but had treated the disorders as separate outcomes. The studies of incretin drugs were observational cohorts of people with type 2 diabetes or obesity, which reported more frozen shoulder and, in several studies, fewer diagnoses of carpal tunnel syndrome among users; such comparisons are open to confounding by indication and to differences in health-care contact between treated and untreated patients. No study had examined whether these disorders share a common genetic structure or had assessed them in randomised trial data. Mendelian randomisation showed that genetically higher adiposity increases liability to carpal tunnel syndrome but decreases liability to Dupuytrens disease, an opposite effect reproduced in independent cohorts and in each sex and colocalised at the FTO obesity locus. papers.title: Overlapping yet distinct spatiomolecular profiles across mood disorders and biological sex in the human prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD) exhibit both overlapping and distinct clinical features, including sex differences in prevalence and symptomatology, but how these similarities and differences are reflected at the molecular and cellular level in the human brain remains poorly understood. Within the NVU, transcriptional evidence of impaired vascular integrity was accompanied by astrocytic response profiles in females with MDD and males with BD, with inflammatory responses further evident in females with MDD ( IFITM3 , CEBPD , IL1R1 ). papers.title: ALBIS: simulation of multi-resolution and multi-dimensional spatial transcriptomics data
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies has been accompanied by substantial growth in computational methods, creating an increasing need for systematic and reliable benchmarking, particularly as analyses increasingly extend from individual tissue sections to three-dimensional (3D) tissue reconstruction. Existing benchmarks often rely on a small and similar set of experimentally-derived datasets because they offer a reliable ground truth label, which is hard to find in practice. Simulated or synthetic data provide an alternative, yet most existing simulators either adapt single-cell RNA sequencing models to spatial coordinates or generate individual sections in a two-dimensional (2D) space at predefined resolutions. More recent approaches can simulate 2D and 3D tissues, but generally do not derive multiple spatial resolutions from the same molecular realization. Here, we introduce ALBIS (A mu L ti-resolution B iological I n-silica S imulator for spatial transcriptomics), a statistically grounded and highly customizable framework that generates synthetic ST data from an in silica 3D tissue. ALBIS defines spatially structured cell populations with corresponding markers for gene expression, then initializes individual mRNA molecules in 3D space to create cell-level information with a ground truth 3D coordinate for each molecule and cell. From this common realization, ALBIS cuts the 3D tissue into multiple 2D tissue sections with cell-, bin-, and spot-level measurements, enabling direct comparison across spatial resolutions. Properties of the simulated data, including spatial domains, cell type composition, gene-expression effects, batch effects, measurement resolution, and tissue scale, can be systematically varied, enabling rigorous stress-testing of computational methods under known and increasingly challenging conditions.

papers.title: HetAnn: Cell Type Annotation for Spatial Transcriptomics by Heterogeneous Graph Learning.
papers.abstract: Currently, several new spatial transcriptomics(ST) technologies have attained cellular or even subcellular spatial resolution. Effective methods for annotating cell types are essential for the growing volumes of single-cell ST data. Most of automatic annotation methods for ST data use reference single cell RNA-sequencing(scRNA-seq) data, but how to efficiently integrate spatial information from ST data and gene expression information from ST and scRNA-seq data into a unified model remains a challenge. The difficulty in integrating the single cell multimodal data is that different modalities have different feature spaces, which easily leads to cell type mismatching. In this study, we propose HetAnn, a semi-supervised deep learning method for cell type annotation of ST data. HetAnn learns ST-specific representation by cell graphs accounting for both cell-to-cell spatial distance and gene expression similarity in ST data. HetAnn employs a graph attention network to learn multimodal representation with end-to-end joint training on ST and reference scRNA-seq data. These two comprehensive embeddings enable HetAnn to remove the gap between modalities while preserving cell-type heterogeneity. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of HetAnn compared with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Epitope-diverse autoantibodies induce neutrophil-epithelial niches driving kidney injury in ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis.

papers.title: Cytokine context shapes antigen-presenting and matrix-producing states of cancer-associated fibroblasts.
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) exhibit remarkable functional heterogeneity, with conserved subtypes observed across diverse malignancies. However, their shared roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment (TME) and their dynamic plasticity remain incompletely understood. Across multiple solid tumors, apCAFs were associated with enhanced anti-tumor immune features and favorable prognosis, whereas mCAFs were associated with immunosuppressive characteristics and poorer clinical outcomes. Functionally, patient-derived apCAFs promoted T-cell migration, proliferation, and activation, whereas mCAFs suppressed these responses in vitro. Pan-cancer analyses further revealed a strong inverse correlation between apCAF and mCAF abundance across tumor tissues. Mechanistically, IFN-γ and TGF-β-associated signaling contexts were linked to distinct CAF transcriptional programs, with IFN-γ promoting apCAF-associated features and TGF-β favoring mCAF-associated features, suggesting a potential role of cytokine context in shaping CAF state heterogeneity. Clinically, apCAFs correlated with favorable immunotherapy response, whereas mCAFs predicted poor therapeutic outcomes. Collectively, these findings identify conserved immunomodulatory CAF subtypes across cancers, reveal distinct cytokine-associated CAF programs, and support stromal reprogramming as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

papers.title: Single-Cell and Spatial Multi-Omics in Small-Intestinal Homeostasis and Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury: Current Advances, Applications, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: The intestinal tract acts as a dynamic barrier between the external and internal environments, and intestinal homeostasis fundamentally influences human health. This homeostasis depends on complex interactions among the epithelium, immune cells, and microbiota. Intestinal ischemia/reperfusion (II/R) disrupts these interactions and can cause local barrier failure and distant organ injury. However, the transition of the intestinal microenvironment from homeostasis to injury and repair remains incompletely characterized. This narrative review summarizes single-cell RNA sequencing, single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial multi-omics, including their underlying methods. We compare intestinal reference atlases with direct II/R studies and examine how these approaches complement bulk sequencing and histology. Human intestinal atlases reveal spatially organized epithelial states, whereas experimental II/R studies identify altered Paneth-cell states, endothelial regenerative signals, and epithelial stress responses. These findings differ in their model systems, sampling times, and degree of functional validation. Dissociation bias, batch effects, limited biological replication, spatial resolution, and uncertain integration across modalities constrain interpretation. Most disease-specific evidence remains preclinical, and inferred cell interactions should not be equated with demonstrated therapeutic mechanisms. Translation will require standardized human sampling, spatial and protein-level validation, causal perturbation, and prospective assessment of clinically accessible markers. Single-cell and spatial omics can therefore refine mechanistic hypotheses and guide validation in II/R, but currently do not constitute established clinical diagnostic or treatment pathways.

At each study visit, SFDI, high-frequency ultrasound, and durometry were done in all participants, and mRSS was assessed in patients with systemic sclerosis. Optional forearm biopsy and blood collection was done at baseline in consenting participants. papers.title: Recent advances in cancer-associated fibroblasts in colorectal cancer: functional subtypes, spatiotemporal dynamics and therapeutic targets.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a malignant tumour with an extremely high global incidence rate; its development and progression are closely linked to fibroblasts within the tumour microenvironment (TME). In recent years, single-cell and spatial multi-omics technologies have revealed the high heterogeneity of fibroblasts in colorectal cancer and identified multiple subtypes with either oncogenic or tumour-suppressive functions. Within the TME, these fibroblast states have been associated with key processes in tumour initiation, progression, metastasis, and treatment resistance, although direct functional evidence for many of them remains to be established. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the origins, differentiation and activation trajectories, stage-associated distribution patterns, and spatial characteristics of fibroblasts, with a focus on newly identified functional states and their distributions across primary and metastatic CRC. Furthermore, given that the efficacy of current clinical treatments for fibroblasts remains less than satisfactory, there is still a need to develop effective targeted therapies for these newly identified subtypes in the future.

papers.title: Medulloblastoma Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Tumor Microenvironment Heterogeneity With High-Density Progenitor Cell Regions Correlating With High-Risk Disease.

The tumor microenvironment (TME) influences progression and therapy response, presenting a promising target for therapeutic advances. Samples at diagnosis were stratified into high- and standard-risk groups. Spatial data were analyzed for spatial proximity to other cell types, cell-cell communication networks, and expression of cell cycle dormancy signatures. Findings were validated using immunohistochemistry in the same cohort.ResultsOur analyses revealed intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity within the TME, comprising tumor-associated astrocytes (TAAs), macrophages (TAMs), stromal components, and distinct subpopulations of MB cells at different stages of neuronal differentiation and cell cycle progression. papers.title: Molecular landscape of anaplastic transformation in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with anaplastic features is a rare and highly aggressive subtype with an extremely poor prognosis. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying anaplastic transformation remain poorly understood. To characterize the anaplastic transformation molecular landscape, we analyzed genomic alterations in 5,997 conventional PDAC and 41 anaplastic carcinoma cases from the Memorial Sloan Kettering-Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable Cancer Targets (MSK-IMPACT) cohort. Additionally, four PDAC samples from the Kyorin cohort with both tubular and anaplastic components were subjected to spatial transcriptomics using the Visium platform. Differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed to identify key molecular drivers. Genomic analysis revealed higher KRAS (90 versus 75%), TP53 (85 versus 60%), and CDKN2A (50 versus 30%) mutation frequencies, but notably fewer SMAD4 mutations (5 versus 20%; p = 0.022), in anaplastic carcinoma than in conventional PDAC. Spatial transcriptomics identified distinct molecular signatures, with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathways significantly enriched in anaplastic regions. Levels of ELF3, an epithelial transcription factor, were consistently downregulated in all anaplastic components. Importantly, we detected a strong inverse correlation between SMAD4 and ELF3 expression in both the bulk RNA sequencing cohort and spatial transcriptomic data. Functional validation using the KC-shSmad4 mouse model demonstrated that increased Smad4 suppressed Elf3 expression and promoted mesenchymal reprogramming. Our findings suggest a novel SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis that may contribute to anaplastic transformation in PDAC. The retention of SMAD4 functions coupled with ELF3 downregulation may promote EMT and contribute to tumor dedifferentiation. This SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis may provide a framework for identifying therapeutic vulnerabilities in this aggressive PDAC variant and further highlight the utility of spatial transcriptomics for understanding tumor heterogeneity. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

papers.title: Machine learning and multi-omics analyses reveal CLDN1 as a candidate marker associated with colorectal cancer invasion and nutlin-3a (-) response.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveColorectal cancer (CRC) is molecularly, cellularly and spatially heterogeneous, and current staging systems and biomarkers incompletely explain prognosis and treatment response. Candidate genes were prioritized by differential expression, model importance and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance. papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal a DLL4-associated tip-like endothelial niche linked to neoadjuvant chemotherapy non-response in muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
papers.abstract: Chemotherapy non-response remains a major challenge in bladder cancer, yet the endothelial states and intercellular communication programs associated with treatment failure remain poorly understood. Elevated DLL4 expression was associated with chemotherapy non-response and unfavorable survival. In a separate prognostic analysis, a DLL4-positive TipEC_2-associated risk model stratified patients by overall survival in TCGA-BLCA and GSE13507. Collectively, these findings identify a DLL4-associated tip-like endothelial niche linked to chemotherapy non-response and suggest DLL4-NOTCH3 signaling as a potential molecular link between vascular remodeling and treatment resistance in bladder cancer.

papers.title: Hypoxia-mediated glioblastoma cell-macrophage crosstalk via the TIMP1-LRP1 axis induces immunosuppression.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma is characterized by hypoxia, immune suppression, and poor clinical outcome. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, human glioblastoma specimens, and murine models to define hypoxia-enriched tumor-associated macrophages (hTAMs) and their interaction with hypoxic glioblastoma cells (hGBM cells). hTAMs displayed an immunosuppressive transcriptional program, were enriched in mesenchymal glioblastoma, and were associated with worse survival. These findings identify a hypoxia-associated tumor-macrophage signaling axis that links glioblastoma adaptation to immune suppression and supports therapeutic targeting of the tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Intranasal HSV‑1 infection drives region‑specific interferon‑dominant microglial remodeling.
papers.abstract: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is a neurotropic pathogen capable of invading the central nervous system (CNS) and is associated with chronic neuroinflammation, cognitive impairment, and neurodegenerative disease. While microglia orchestrate the initial immune response to HSV‑1, the molecular mechanisms that regulate their sustained neuroinflammatory activity in vivo remain poorly understood. To define the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms that shape microglial responses during acute HSV-1 infection in vivo, we have, for the first time, integrated single‑nucleus RNA sequencing, chromatin accessibility profiling, and spatial proteomics and transcriptomics in an intranasal HSV‑1 infection model. Single-cell multiome analysis of CD11b⁺ nuclei identified transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct microglial and macrophage populations. HSV-1 infection redistributed monocyte-lineage states, with a marked overrepresentation of interferon (IFN)‑responsive microglia and macrophage-associated populations characterized by amplification of Stat1/2, Irf1, and Cebpb rather than reflecting uniform inflammatory activation. In parallel, homeostatic microglial gene signatures (e.g., ApoE, Cst3) were reduced following HSV-1 infection. Spatial transcriptomics localized HSV‑1 antigen to discrete brainstem regions, which were enriched for predicted STAT1/2, IRF1, and CEBPB‑regulated targets identified through single‑nuclei analysis, demonstrating that these inferred transcriptional networks are activated within anatomically defined regions in vivo. Complementary spatial proteomics further confirmed increased microglial activation and astrocytic responses specifically within HSV-1 antigen-positive regions. Together, these integrated multiomic analyses demonstrate that HSV-1 induces localized transcriptional and epigenetic remodeling of microglia dominated by IFN-driven regulatory programs and a loss of homeostatic signatures. By linking single-cell regulatory architecture to spatially restricted tissue responses, our findings provide mechanistic insight into how localized viral infection sustains neuroinflammation, contributing to long-term neurological vulnerability and neurodegenerative disease risk.

papers.title: From HPV infection to cervical precancer: Molecular mechanisms, immune microenvironment and emerging technologies.
papers.abstract: Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women globally, with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection as the primary etiological factor. Cervical precancerous lesions, including high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and adenocarcinoma in situ, represent the critical window for intervention prior to invasive cancer development. However, additional factors such as immunosuppression, smoking, and microbiome composition also play crucial roles in the development of cervical precancerous lesions. While HPV vaccination, screening, and treatment have reduced cancer incidence, these must be complemented by personalized approaches that target the molecular mechanisms driving carcinogenesis. Key dysregulated tumor suppressors (e.g., p16) and signaling pathways (PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin) highlight the need for advanced therapeutic strategies. The immune microenvironment also plays a critical role in cancer progression, suggesting potential for immunotherapy. Promising biomarkers like p16, Ki67, and microRNAs require integration with technologies such as single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics for deeper insights into tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment dynamics. Additionally, while deep learning models hold promise in improving diagnostic accuracy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), challenges such as data variability and interpretability need addressing. In conclusion, incorporating genomics, transcriptomics, immunotherapy, and artificial intelligence will enable more personalized and effective interventions, ultimately reducing the global burden of cervical cancer.

papers.title: Computational deconvolution of drug sensitivity via single-cell-to-bulk transcriptome mapping.
papers.abstract: Analyses routinely conducted in both fundamental research and biomedical studies often report aggregate signals derived from heterogeneous mixtures of cells. These mixtures reflect the intrinsic anatomical and functional complexity of the tissues and organs from which they are derived. Such bulk measurements obscure cell-specific signals, thereby hindering accurate interpretation of the underlying biological processes. Here, we introduce CLIMB and CLIFF, a two-step machine-learning framework that deconvolves bulk RNA-seq into cell-type composition and expression, and then resolves bulk drug sensitivity measurements into cell subtype- and single-cell-specific profiles. We first validate CLIMB using in-vitro mixtures of leukemic cell lines with experimentally known cell-type proportions, then extend this validation to large-scale, cross-dataset pseudo-bulk analyses built from independent scRNA-seq references across two disease contexts and five cancer types - mimicking the reference-to-target mismatches encountered in real applications - and show that CLIMB accurately infers the cellular composition of bulk samples, outperforming state-of-the-art bulk deconvolution methods. We emphasize CLIMB's effectiveness in acute myeloid leukemia, where it offers highly accurate estimation of leukemic stem cell fractions across three test datasets and three patient cohorts. We then validate CLIFF, our algorithm for estimating cell subtype- and single-cell-specific drug sensitivity, first on the same in-vitro cell line mixtures using experimentally measured drug responses, and then through in-depth, realistic-scale pseudo-bulk simulations. We applied our deconvolution strategy to the beatAML cohort dataset, currently the most extensive database of ex-vivo drug screening data. This analysis generated a cell subtype-resolved drug sensitivity landscape for 121 compounds, revealing multiple compounds putatively active against leukemic stem cells, including midostaurin, A-674563, SNS-032, and foretinib. Collectively, our work introduces a general computational framework for resolving bulk functional measurements at cell-type and single-cell resolution, providing an attractive new computational tool for drug development and precision medicine.

papers.title: Omega-3 fatty acids reprogram tumor-associated macrophage cytokine signaling and suppress pancreatic cancer growth.
papers.abstract: Dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) shape inflammatory signaling within the pancreatic tumor microenvironment (TME), but the cellular mechanisms underlying their effects on tumor progression remain unclear. Using orthotopic models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), we show that omega-3 (n-3) and omega-6 (n-6) PUFAs are differentially incorporated into tumor lipid pools, generating spatially heterogeneous lipid microenvironments. While an n-6-enriched diet accelerated PDAC growth, an n-3-enriched diet suppressed tumor growth in a T cell-independent manner. Examining inflammatory effects in PDAC tumors, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 family members, and single-cell and spatial analyses identified tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) as the primary diet-responsive population. Indeed, selective conversion of n-6 to n-3 fatty acids within myeloid cells using an inducible fat-1 transgene, which encodes an n-3 desaturase that converts n-6 to n-3 PUFAs in vivo, was sufficient to suppress tumor growth, whereas fibroblast-restricted conversion had no effect. This finding is the first to formally establish that cellular origin of PUFA metabolism within the TME is a key determinant of tumor progression and identifies TAMs as critical mediators of n-3-dependent tumor suppression. Furthermore, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced Arg1+ immunosuppressive TAMs and promoted C1q+ and MHC-II+ antigen-presenting TAM populations enriched for antigen processing machinery and T cell-recruiting chemokines, alongside reduced IL-6 family cytokine production. Together, these findings establish macrophages as key mediators of n-3-driven tumor control and define a mechanism by which dietary lipids remodel cytokine signaling in the PDAC microenvironment.

papers.title: The S-technique: A Novel Dense Polytetrafluoroethylene-assisted Surgical Technique for Peri-implant Keratinized Mucosa Preservation - A Case Review.
papers.abstract: AbstractImmediate implant placement following tooth extraction often leads to peri-implant defects that require guided bone regeneration (GBR) to achieve complete bone fill and stable osseointegration. Conventional GBR techniques typically rely on primary flap closure, coronal advancement, and additional soft-tissue grafting, which increase surgical complexity and patient morbidity. The S-Technique was introduced to enable simultaneous hard and soft-tissue regeneration under open-healing conditions while preserving the mucogingival junction. A patient presented with a grossly decayed, painful, vertically fractured, nonrestorable maxillary right second premolar (tooth 15). After atraumatic extraction and immediate implant placement, a peri-implant gap defect with limited soft-tissue availability was noted. GBR was performed using particulate xenograft and a resorbable collagen membrane. A dense polytetrafluoroethylene membrane was then placed according to the S-technique protocol, allowing secondary epithelialization without primary closure. Healing progressed uneventfully. At 4 months, clinical assessment showed complete coverage of the peri-implant site, an adequate band of keratinized mucosa, improved soft-tissue contour, a favorable emergence profile, and stable peri-implant architecture. Prosthetic rehabilitation resulted in satisfactory esthetic and functional outcomes with maintained bone support. This case demonstrates the S-Technique as a minimally invasive dual-layer membrane approach for simultaneous hard and soft-tissue regeneration around immediate implants. By eliminating the need for primary closure and autogenous soft-tissue grafting, it offers a predictable alternative for managing peri-implant defects in sites with limited soft-tissue availability, while promoting keratinized mucosa formation and stable peri-implant tissue integration.

papers.title: Ten years and beyond: Long-term dental implant survival, success, and biological health-A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo update dental implant failure and survival estimates beyond 10 years and examine how success definitions and biological outcomes affect interpretation of long-term performance.Materials and methodsRandomized controlled trials, prospective cohorts, and retrospective cohorts with at least 10 years of follow-up were included. Failure proportions were pooled by study design using random-effects models with clustering corrections and prediction intervals. Sensitivity analyses assessed influential studies, risk of bias, surface era, and clustering assumptions. Success, probing depth (PD), marginal bone loss (MBL), and peri-implantitis were summarized descriptively.ResultsThirty-four studies including 7522 patients and 20 445 implants were analyzed. Pooled failure was 5.1% in prospective studies (95% CI, 3.0%-8.7%), 4.9% in retrospective studies (95% CI, 3.3%-7.1%), and 4.8% in randomized trials (95% CI, 3.2%-7.1%), corresponding to survival of approximately 94.9%, 95.1%, and 95.2%, respectively. Success averaged 85.1% across 14 studies, but definitions varied substantially. Descriptive means were 2.99 mm for PD, 1.30 mm for MBL, and 10.8% for implant-level peri-implantitis (range, 3.0%-39.9%).ConclusionsDental implants are highly durable in terms of retention, with approximately 95% survival after 10-25 years. However, high survival does not establish long-term biological health or true treatment success: success rates were lower and definition-dependent, and peri-implant disease showed substantial variability. Retention is therefore a necessary but insufficient endpoint for judging long-term implant therapy.Clinical relevanceLong-term assessment should integrate biological, radiographic, technical, functional, and patient-centered outcomes.

papers.abstract: Mechanical debridement of implant surfaces is limited by implant geometry and defect-related access restrictions. Surface-site distribution also differed within each protocol in Class 1B defects (p ≤ 0.006). Exploratory SEM-EDS observations of individual specimens showed differences in surface appearance. papers.title: Zoledronic acid-loaded dissolvable microneedle patch for targeted regulation of osteoblast/osteoclast homeostasis as a potential treatment for peri-implantitis.
papers.abstract: Peri-implantitis is a major cause of dental implant failure, characterized by localized bone resorption driven by chronic inflammatory disruption of the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activities, which ultimately leads to implant loosening and loss. Zoledronic acid (ZA) exerts potent inhibitory effects on osteoclasts and displays favorable bone-targeting properties; however, systemic administration of ZA carries a high risk of adverse reactions. To overcome this drawback, we fabricated hyaluronic acid-based dissolving microneedles loaded with zoledronic acid (ZA-DMNs) for local transmucosal delivery. This design aims to regulate the local osteoblast-osteoclast balance while eliminating systemic side effects to the greatest extent possible. The as-prepared ZA-DMNs possessed sufficient mechanical strength (withstanding a force of 0.15 N at half-height compression, exceeding the 0.1 N insertion threshold) and achieved a mucosal penetration depth of 140 μm, ensuring efficient transmucosal drug permeation. After insertion into mucosal tissue, the microneedle tips dissolved rapidly, releasing roughly 80% of the encapsulated ZA within 48 h. The liberated ZA binds tightly to bone surfaces with high affinity, locally suppressing osteoclast differentiation and bone resorptive activity. Furthermore, ZA-DMNs successfully rescued osteogenic function impaired by inflammatory microenvironments, and CCK-8 and live/dead staining assays confirmed their favorable biocompayibility. Taken together, these results preliminarily indicate that ZA-DMNs represent a promising local transmucosal delivery platform of ZA for the management of bone loss induced by peri-implantitis.

papers.title: Ten-eleven translocation 3 activates the TGF-β-like ligand Scube3 to promote renal fibrosis: mechanism and translational potential.
papers.abstract: Resident renal fibroblasts are a predominant source for myofibroblasts that produce ECM to contribute to renal fibrosis in the course of chronic kidney disease (CKD). The mechanism whereby fibroblast-myofibroblast transition (FMyT) is driven remains incompletely understood. In the present study, we investigated the involvement of ten-eleven translocation 3 (TET3) in regulating FMyT and renal fibrosis focusing on the regulatory mechanism and translational potential. We report that TET3 deletion in primary renal fibroblasts dampened myofibroblast transition in response to pro-fibrogenic stimuli. Consistently, conditional deletion of TET3 in quiescent fibroblasts (driven by the Col1a2-Cre) or in myofibroblasts (driven by the Postn-Cre) equally attenuated renal fibrosis in mice. Integrated transcriptomic analysis combining RNA-seq and CUT&Tag-seq uncovered signal peptide CUB-EGF-like domain-containing protein 3 (Scube3) as a novel downstream target for TET3. Co-culture assay confirmed that Scube3 mediated intercellular crosstalk and promoted fibroblast activation in an autocrine/paracrine manner. Importantly, myofibroblast-specific Scube3 depletion significantly ameliorated renal fibrosis in mice. Finally, a small-molecule TET3 degrader Bobcat339 suppressed FMyT in vitro and mitigated renal fibrosis in vivo. Our data support a role for TET3 in renal fibrosis and provide proof-of-concept that targeting the TET3-Scube3 axis may yield novel therapeutic solutions for treating CKD.

papers.title: Clinical translation of polymeric microneedles for bioactive nanovesicle delivery in hypertrophic scar remodeling.
papers.abstract: The clinical translation of polymeric microneedle (MN)-based delivery systems for fibrotic diseases remains largely unexplored despite extensive preclinical advances. The dense extracellular matrix of pathological scars constitutes a formidable biophysical barrier that limits homogeneous macromolecular permeation. Here, we conducted a prospective, single-center, open-label, single-arm study evaluating a 12-week protocol combining microplasma radiofrequency (RF), poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) MNs, and topical milk-derived bioactive nanovesicles (mBNVs) in 26 patients with hypertrophic scars. Clinical scales and multimodal imaging were used to assess treatment-associated changes. At week 12, the combined protocol was associated with reductions in VSS and POSAS Patient Scale scores, scar stiffness and thickness, and dermoscopic vascular and pigmentation densities. MN-induced microchannels underwent rapid closure, treatment-related reactions were mild and transient, and no serious or systemic adverse events were observed. Collectively, these findings support the short-term feasibility, tolerability, and preliminary clinical activity of the combined protocol, offering a safe and non-steroidal paradigm for mechanically resistant pathological tissues.

papers.title: Maxillary canine angulation and position before alveolar bone grafting in patients with unilateral complete cleft lip and palate a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The rate of maxillary canine displacement is reported to be higher in patients with cleft compared to normal population. The aim of this study is to compare the displacement tendency of developing maxillary canines in patients with unilateral complete cleft lip and palate (UCLP) versus non-cleft controls before secondary alveolar bone grafting or orthodontic treatment. Design: A cross-sectional observational study. Setting : University orthodontic clinic. Materials and Methods : Eighty-six children aged (8–12 years) were included: 43 with non-syndromic UCLP and 43 non-cleft controls with skeletal Class I relationships. The percentage of patients with high-risk alpha angle (> 30 degrees ) of maxillary canines was assessed between study groups as well as between cleft side and non-cleft side in group. The canine horizontal and vertical sector positions were also evaluated. Results Maxillary canines in patients with UCLP demonstrated significantly greater alpha angles than those in controls. The odds of an alpha angle > 30 degrees were approximately 15-fold higher in patients with UCLP than in controls and approximately 11-fold higher on cleft than non-cleft sides. Vertical canine position also differed significantly, with a greater proportion of canines occupying more apical sectors on cleft sides. Horizontal sector distribution did not differ significantly between groups. No significant association was found between lateral-incisor agenesis and alpha angle. Conclusions Before secondary alveolar bone grafting or orthodontic intervention, UCLP was associated with greater maxillary canine angulation and a more apical vertical position, particularly on the cleft side. These findings suggest that panoramic assessment of canine angulation and vertical position may help identify developing canines at increased risk of ectopic eruption. Longitudinal studies are required to determine their predictive value for subsequent canine impaction.

papers.title: Effects of Oral Catalpol on Alveolar Bone Regeneration in a Rat Model of Alveolar Ridge Preservation
papers.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the effects of oral catalpol administration on alveolar bone regeneration in a rat model of alveolar ridge preservation (ARP) following tooth extraction. Fifty male Sprague–Dawley rats were randomly assigned to five groups (n = 10/group): Extraction, ARP, ARP + Low-dose Catalpol (25 mg/kg), ARP + Medium-dose Catalpol (50 mg/kg), and ARP + High-dose Catalpol (100 mg/kg). ARP involved Bio-Oss grafting and membrane coverage. Five rats per group were euthanized at 4 and 8 weeks postoperatively. Bone microarchitecture was evaluated using micro-computed tomography, serum bone turnover markers were measured by ELISA, and tissue morphology was examined using Masson's trichrome staining. At 4 weeks, the ARP + High-dose Catalpol group exhibited significantly higher BMD, BV/TV, and Tb.N and lower Tb.Sp than the ARP group. At 8 weeks, BMD and BV/TV remained significantly higher in the ARP + High-dose Catalpol group. Catalpol administration was associated with increased serum BALP and OCN levels and decreased CTX-I levels. Histological observations suggested enhanced bone formation following catalpol treatment. These findings suggest that oral catalpol may promote alveolar bone regeneration following ARP, with the greatest improvements observed at 100 mg/kg.

papers.title: An Explainable Multimodal Deep-Learning Model Using Histopathological Image and Clinical Information for Prognosis Prediction in Colorectal Cancer: A Multi-Center Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Accurate prognostication is crucial for the individualized management of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), while the accuracy and interpretability of current models still need to be improved. This study aims to develop and validate an explainable multimodal model for precise survival prediction. 3381 patients with resected CRC are enrolled from three medical centers, and a multimodal deep-learning framework integrating clinical variables and histopathological images is developed. The multimodal model exhibits significantly more robust performance than unimodal models in prognosis prediction across all of the cohorts. By stratifying patients into low-risk and high-risk groups based on the model-derived risk scores, high-risk patients exhibit worse outcomes, and the stratification remains an independent prognostic factor in multivariable Cox regression. The model also identifies patients with markedly poorer survival among the stage II/III subgroup. Adjuvant chemotherapy demonstrates benefits in high-risk patients with stage III CRC but not in the low-risk group. Multi-omic analyses disclose that low-risk tumors are characterized by enhanced adaptive immune responses, whereas high-risk tumors exhibit stronger angiogenesis and higher exhaustion scores of T cells, reflecting a hypoxic and immunosuppressive microenvironment. These results support the potential of the multimodal model to effectively predict survival outcomes in resected CRC with great explainability.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics of pediatric tuberculosis lymph nodes reveals a conserved hypoxia–SPP1 niche
papers.abstract: Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) often presents as primary disease involving the mediastinal lymph nodes; however, its granuloma microenvironment remains poorly characterized because these population patient tissues are rarely available for study. Here, we use spatial transcriptomics to profile 60 granulomas from four children aged 4 to 36 months. We identified nine recurrent transcriptional microenvironments shared across granulomas, despite their marked histological heterogeneity. One macrophage-rich microenvironment showed strong hypoxia-associated activity and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) enrichment. This microenvironment was present in both non-necrotic and necrotic lesions and overlapped with a Mtb-persistence macrophage signature previously identified in murine TB lymph nodes. Pathway analysis revealed the enrichment of both antimicrobial and regulatory programs within this microenvironment, suggesting partial immune control rather than uniform inflammatory or suppressive activity in this region. SPP1 expression was associated with regions enriched for both M1- and M2-like macrophages, suggesting a macrophage program that extends beyond conventional polarization classifications and may be influenced by the local granuloma microenvironment. We further observed a similar spatial association between hypoxia-associated activity and SPP1 expression in an independent adult TB dataset (pooled Spearman ρ=0.65) and validated this association at protein level by multiplex immunofluorescence in our pediatric TB granuloma sample. Overall, this study identified a hypoxia-associated SPP1 -enriched microenvironment that may contribute to incomplete bacterial clearance and could provide a framework for evaluating host-directed strategies to enhance sterilizing immunity without exacerbating tissue damage.

papers.title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions
papers.abstract: BackgroundMalignant effusions are clinically accessible yet underutilized sources of metastatic tumor cells. However, abundant background immune cells complicate tumor cell isolation and molecular characterization. We integrate AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free tumor cell enrichment with genomic profiling to characterize phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. MethodsWe applied a pre-trained deep learning model to brightfield images of single cells from malignant effusions of 10 patients with metastatic breast cancer to extract morphological features, quantify tumor cell fraction (TCF), and guide label-free microfluidic enrichment. We profiled copy-number alterations and somatic mutations in enriched tumor cell fractions and compared them with available matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors. ResultsAI-powered single-cell morphological analysis identified putative tumor cells in all 10 patients (median TCF, 5.4%; range, 0.51-15.8%; n = 25 samples). AI estimates of major immune-cell populations varied across patients and samples and correlated with flow cytometry measurements (n = 21 paired samples, Pearson r = 0.69-0.75). Unsupervised analysis identified four tumor cell morphotypes, revealing intra- and inter-patient morphological heterogeneity and longitudinal variation in morphotype composition. Genomic profiling of enriched tumor cell fractions by low-pass whole-genome sequencing (n = 26 samples) and whole-exome sequencing (n = 24 samples) identified copy-number alterations and somatic mutations, with tumor fraction influencing genomic signal strength. Comparisons of genomic profiles from tumor cell-enriched fractions with matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors revealed shared genomic alterations, providing orthogonal support for tumor origin and relatedness, while differences across analytes revealed genomic divergence and tumor heterogeneity. ConclusionAI-powered analysis leverages single-cell morphology for tumor cell identification and label-free enrichment, while integration with genomic profiling enables simultaneous interrogation of phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. This approach expands the potential of malignant effusions for liquid biopsy applications and biomarker development and discovery.

papers.title: The Clinical and Cellular Landscape of DKK1 in Osteosarcoma
papers.abstract: BackgroundDickkopf-1 (DKK1) is a secreted protein that acts as a Wnt antagonist and is implicated in osteosarcoma progression. Elevated circulating DKK1 levels have been described at OS diagnosis, but its circulating dynamics, prognostic relevance, and cellular distribution remain incompletely characterized. MethodsWe analysed longitudinal plasma DKK1 in 34 patients using mixed-effects models, evaluated DKK1 expression and survival in two independent transcriptomic cohorts, and examined cellular and tissue distribution using single-cell transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry. Cultured mesenchymal stem cells were assessed as potential nonmalignant sources. ResultsCirculating DKK1 declined by 12.4% per 30-day period during treatment, without significant changes detected around primary tumour resection or relapse. Metastatic presentation and poor histologic response were associated with higher estimated DKK1 levels. Higher tumour DKK1 expression was associated with worse overall and metastasis-free survival (pooled HRs per SD increase: 1.35 [95% CI 1.02-1.78] and 1.48 [1.06-2.07], respectively). DKK1 transcripts were predominantly detected in malignant cells across multiple subpopulations and protein staining was enriched in osteoid and matrix-rich regions of primary tumours. ConclusionsTumour DKK1 expression is associated with adverse outcomes, while circulating concentration decline over treatment time. These findings support further prognostic evaluation and investigation of the associations among DKK1 expression and production, tissue localisation, and circulating levels.
